description:
Objective:
The U.S. Army is seeking innovative force sustainment solutions from eligible small businesses across the U.S. through the xTech Kinetic Reach competition. This platform offers participants the opportunity to engage with the Department of War (DoW), earn prize money and submit a Direct to Phase II Army Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) proposal.

The U.S. Army FUZE xTech Program, in partnership with the U.S. Army Europe and Africa (USAREUR-AF) and Global Tactical Edge Acquisition Directorate (G-TEAD) is executing the xTech|Kinetic Reach competition as part of the G-TEAD Accelerated Capability Event (ACE) series. xTech|Kinetic Reach addresses the growing uncrewed aerial system (UAS) threat by identifying high-potential solutions and accelerating transition through funding and integration into live USAREUR-AF-led exercises. Integrating into a USAREUR-AF-led exercise is critical to: (1) validate capabilities under operationally realistic conditions, (2) inform acquisition and integration decisions, and (3) address near-term gaps in autonomous ground operations and effects delivery in contested environments.

The Army recognizes that the DoW must enhance engagements with U.S. small businesses by (1) understanding the spectrum of world-class technologies being developed commercially that may benefit the DoW; (2) integrating the sector of non-traditional innovators into the DoW Science and Technology (S&T) ecosystem; and (3) providing expertise and feedback to accelerate, mature, and transition technologies of interest to the DoW.

Description:
xTech|Kinetic Reach is a focused open-topic competition designed to identify cutting-edge technology solutions that will drive significant advancements in military capabilities while addressing complex challenges and enhancing national security. In largescale combat operations, U.S. Army forces must sustain dispersed, continuously moving formations while operating inside highly contested environments characterized by persistent observation, long range fires, electromagnetic interference, degraded mobility corridors, and severely constrained logistics. Current sustainment and recovery methods rely heavily on manned systems that are increasingly vulnerable, slow to adapt, and unable to meet the demands of operations conducted near or within the Autonomous Zone. The Army requires a suite of interoperable, autonomous or minimally manned capabilities - spanning ground and air distribution, power generation, forward arming and refueling, and vehicle recovery - that can operate with minimal oversight, low signatures, reduced logistical burden, and seamless command and control (C2) integration. These capabilities must sustain tempo, reduce soldier exposure, and ensure survivability and mission continuity across the entire sustainment and recovery enterprise in high-threat, GPS and communications degraded environments where traditional methods are no longer feasible or survivable.

The Army is seeking to evaluate capabilities that demonstrate performance in one of six (6) capability areas, and meet the following criteria for its capability area:

Topic 1: Uncrewed Ground Payload Transportation

Topic 2: Autonomous container Handling/Movement System

Topic 3: Future Power Generation

Topic 4: Autonomous UAV/UGV Forward Arming and Refueling Point (FARP) System

Topic 5: Uncrewed Aerial Payload Transportation

Topic 6: Uncrewed, Automated, Ground Recovery System

Full competition details including details on these 6 topic areas of interest can be found in Appendix A section of the xTech|Kinetic Reach competition RFI here: https://www.xtech.army.mil/competitions/.

The U.S. Army intends to award up to $1,500,000 in cash prizes throughout the competition. Produce prototype solutions that will be easy to operate by a Soldier. These products will be provided to select Army units for testing and experimentation with end Users in a realistic field environment. Feedback from testing and experimentation will be provided directly to Small Businesses to iterate rapidly on recommended modifications or improvements for Army operational use. In addition, companies will work with Army partners to develop a draft technology transition and commercialization plan for DoW and commercial markets.

title: Ground-Based Affordable Mass (G-BAM)
summary: The United States currently faces an "unprecedented" military buildup by China and increasing air and missile threats that demand a robust deterrent. However, the current inventory of long-range strike weapons is dominated by high-cost, low-volume systems or aging strategic assets like the Minuteman III, which dates back to the 1960s.
description:
Objective:
The United States currently faces an "unprecedented" military buildup by China and increasing air and missile threats that demand a robust deterrent. However, the current inventory of long-range strike weapons is dominated by high-cost, low-volume systems or aging strategic assets like the Minuteman III, which dates back to the 1960s. The lack of a cost-effective, ground-launched payload delivery system prevents the Joint Force from achieving producibility at scale, leaving the U.S. vulnerable in high-intensity, multi-domain environments where high-end munitions would be rapidly depleted. The objective of this topic is to facilitate innovative research on low-cost, rapidly manufacturable, payload delivery systems.

Description:
The Department of War (DoW) is pivotally shifting toward "affordable mass" to counter peer adversaries who are rapidly expanding their military capabilities. While hypersonic systems offer high speeds, their exorbitant costs—exceeding $50 million per round—limit the military's ability to achieve the "magazine depth" necessary for prolonged conflict. This project proposes a ground-based, non-hypersonic, long-range precision payload delivery system that leverages low-cost production methods and commercial technologies to provide a scalable, high-volume alternative that is a tenth of the price of current high-end munitions. NOTE: The following topic number, ARM26BX04-DV011 – Ground-Based Affordable Mass (G-BAM), in this release is tied to a Defense Innovation Unit (DIU) Challenge Commercial Solutions Openings. The DIU G-BAM Challenge will be used to identify small business concerns that meet the criteria for a potential SBIR Direct-to-Phase II (DP2) award under this topic. Winners selected from the DIU G-BAM Challenge will be the only firms eligible to submit an SBIR DP2 proposal under this topic. Proposals submitted to this topic by non-winners of the DIU G-BAM Challenge will not be evaluated.

How to Apply: Visit the DIU Open Solicitations page to read the full Challenge Announcement, topic details, and application instructions here:

https://www.diu.mil/work-with-us/open-solicitations

Phase I:
This topic is accepting Direct to Phase II submissions for a cost limit up to $2,000,000 and an 18-24-month period of performance.

Phase II:
This topic is a DP2 topic. In order for proposers to submit a DP2 proposal, they must provide justification documentation to substantiate that the scientific and technical merit and feasibility described above has been met and describes the potential military and/or commercial applications. Documentation should include all relevant information including, but not limited to: technical reports, test data, prototype designs/models, and performance goals/results. This justification must be provided during the DIU G-BAM Challenge in order to be selected as a winner and eligible to submit a DP2 proposal under this topic The results from the DIU G-BAM Challenge demonstration event, will be used to determine eligibility for DP2.

The objectives during Phase II are to produce prototype solutions that will be easy to operate by a Soldier. These products will be provided to select Army or other Department of War (DoW) units for testing and experimentation with end Users in a realistic field environment. Feedback from testing and experimentation will be provided directly to Small Businesses to iterate rapidly on recommended modifications or improvements for Army operational use. In addition, companies will work with Army partners to develop a draft technology transition and commercialization plan for DoW and commercial markets. Prototype capabilities sought include:

• Cost Efficiency: Cost-per-effect below $500K based on system reliability and mission success rate, with a sub-$250K all-up flyaway cost at scale.
• Producibility: Demonstrate a company manufacturing process capable of producing 100+ units monthly (1,200+ annually), or a credible path to that rate.
• Operational Range: Validate a ground-launched range with an objective of 600+ nm, consistent with DIU’s Area of Interest (AoI) Statement stated preference for extended-range effects.
• Employment: Should not require the Army to develop or modify other systems for employment. Should be a “plug and play” system that easily integrates with existing transport, targeting, and situational awareness systems.
• Payload: Deliver a payload capacity of at least 35 pounds, with a strong preference for greater than 100 pounds.
• Survivability: Demonstrate mission-capability in Denied, Disrupted, Intermittent, and Limited (DDIL) and electronic-warfare (EW)-contested environments.

Reliability: Demonstrate reliability and mission success under representative operational conditions.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
The sub-system technologies developed for low-cost, long-range payload delivery have significant applications in the civilian/commercial aerospace and logistics sectors. The artificial intelligence (AI) and autonomous navigation systems required for these munitions can be adapted for commercial cargo delivery drones and autonomous maritime vessels. Additionally, the push for additive manufacturing and rapid prototyping in the Indo-Pacific region to support these systems can revitalize domestic high-tech manufacturing, providing private companies with advanced production techniques that reduce costs for civilian infrastructure projects. Additionally, this space lends itself to the potential for development of low-cost alternate fuel technologies. Companies participating in the shoot-off are encouraged to propose tech development for manufacturing methods materials/guidance/seekers/alt propulsion, etc. to enhance their products. These are the primary opportunities for commercialization.

title: xTech|Search 10 Competition
summary: xTechSearch is an open-topic competition designed to identify groundbreaking technologies with strong commercial traction that may also provide game-changing capabilities for the Army. This competition will be used to competitively down-select up to 16 finalists who can submit a Phase I Army SBIR proposal for a potential follow-on award of up to $300,000.
description:
Objective:
xTechSearch is an open-topic competition designed to identify groundbreaking technologies with strong commercial traction that may also provide game-changing capabilities for the Army. This competition will be used to competitively down-select up to 16 finalists who can submit a Phase I Army SBIR proposal for a potential follow-on award of up to $300,000.

Description:
The SBIR|STTR Program has aligned technologies that are experiencing rapid commercial traction with critical Army priorities into four portfolios of priority interest for this competition, each with core technology components identified. While xTech|Search encourages submissions aligned to the following SBIR|STTR portfolios and the associated core technology components, the program also welcomes proposals in any other technology domain with the potential to provide a disruptive advantage to the Army:

• Sensors: Electronic devices used to measure physical parameters, often enabling enhanced automation through the Internet of Things.
• Immersive and Wearables: Integration or extension of the real world through digital or simulated reality, such as augmented, virtual, and mixed reality. Wearables focus on smart electronic devices that can be worn by or attached to the user to gather data or provide insight during mission operations.
• AI/ML: Technology that incorporates human intelligence into machines (AI) and allows machines to learn from data without explicit programming (ML).
• Contested Logistics and Sustainment: Strategic and operational technologies that involve planning and executing the movement and maintenance of forces and materials under adversarial conditions.

Note: The topic listed below is part of the xTech|Search 10 Prize Competition. See the full xTech|Search 10 competition RFI here: https://www.xtech.army.mil/competitions/.

xTech|Search 10 will be used to identify small business concerns that meet the criteria for award. Finalists selected from the xTech|Search 10 prize competition will be the only firms eligible to submit a SBIR proposal under the topic listed above. Proposals submitted to the topic listed above by non-finalists or non-participants of the xTech|Search 10 competition will not be evaluated.

Phase I:
This topic is accepting Phase I submissions for a cost limit of $300,000 and a 6-month period of performance. Only finalists of the xTech|Search 10 competition are permitted to submit a phase I proposal for this topic.

Companies will complete a feasibility study that demonstrates the firm’s competitive technical advantage relative to other commercial products (if other products exist) and develop concept plans for how the company’s technology can be applied to Army modernization priority areas. Studies should clearly detail and identify a firm’s technology at both the individual component and system levels, provide supporting literature for technical feasibility, highlight existing performance data, showcase the technology’s application opportunities to a broad base of customers outside the defense space, a market strategy for the commercial space, how the technology directly addresses the Army’s modernization area as well as include a technology development roadmap to demonstrate scientific and engineering viability.

At the end of Phase I, the company will be required to provide a concept demonstration of their technology to demonstrate a high probability that continued design and development will result in a Phase II mature product.

Phase II:
Produce prototype solutions that will be easy to operate by a Soldier. These products will be provided to select Army units for further evaluation by the soldiers. In addition, companies will provide a technology transition and commercialization plan for DOD and commercial markets.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
Complete the maturation of the company’s technology developed in Phase II to TRL 6/7 and produce prototypes to support further development and commercialization. The Army will evaluate each product in a realistic field environment and provide small solutions to stakeholders for further evaluation. Based on soldier evaluations in the field, companies will be requested to update the previously delivered prototypes to meet final design configuration.

Develop a reusable illumination system for high-speed photo-optic data collection used at the Holloman High Speed Test Track (HHSTT) and other sled test tracks.

Description:
The PF300 flash bulbs, that provide high-intensity illumination for high-speed video acquisition, are no longer in production. The objective is to award a contract to a small business to engineer, design, and manufacture a modern, robust, reusable replacement for the legacy PF300 flash bulb. This new system must meet or surpass the existing illumination and performance requirements of the original flash bulbs to ensure seamless integration with current high-speed video systems. The ideal solution would leverage Commercial Off-The-Shelf (COTS) or near-COTS technologies to qualify this project as a direct-to-Phase-II effort. A successful reusable replacement would immediately solve the impending obsolescence issue, securing a reliable illumination source for future missions. Furthermore, transitioning to a reusable system would dramatically reduce consumable cost. This technological update could also pave the way for enhanced capabilities, such as adjustable light intensity and longer duration illumination, offering greater flexibility and improved data quality for high-speed video analysis across various applications

Phase I:
As this is a Direct-to-Phase-II (D2P2) topic, no Phase I awards will be made as a result of this topic. Offerors must demonstrate completion of Phase I feasibility research and development that is not based upon or logically extend from any prior or ongoing federally funded SBIR or STTR work. Prior “Phase I-type” work by other companies has produced similar illumination methods, but not to the requirements needed to operate in the Test Track Environment. The technology exists, but the operating environment of the Test Track is unique enough there is not a readily available product. The Test Track is ready to define requirements up to, but not limited to illumination levels, illumination duration, connectivity and ruggedness.

Phase II:
The Phase II effort should develop a detailed design and operational procedures for a prototype reusable illumination system that meets requirements established by 846 TS Customers. Component level prototypes will be developed and tested to validate performance and mitigate risks prior to the development of the complete system prototype. title: Technical Data Package Modernization for Information Assurance and Secure Data Exchange

The objective of this Directed to Phase II (D2P2) SBIR effort is to develop an innovative, secure, and scalable solution for modernizing Technical Data Packages (TDPs) associated with complex Air and Space Force platforms. This initiative seeks to address challenges in managing large, diverse datasets by enhancing configuration control, ensuring data integrity, and strengthening Information Assurance (IA) in support of mission-critical operations. Specifically, the focus of this phase is to demonstrate the feasibility of advanced technologies that enable secure data lifecycle management and seamless data exchange within operational environments. Proposed solutions should align with Trusted AI and Autonomy modernization priorities by incorporating robust cybersecurity measures and leveraging cutting-edge advancements in autonomy, data management, and secure manufacturing capabilities. Outcomes of this phase are expected to validate technical concepts and establish a functional prototype that meets the operational imperative of readiness to deploy and fight, contributing to future scalability and transition opportunities in operational use cases.

Description:
Background and Problem Statement:

The modernization of Technical Data Packages (TDPs) is imperative to address the Air and Space Force’s operational challenges in securely managing large-scale, complex datasets associated with advanced platforms and their sustainment life cycles. Current TDP systems often lack robust Information Assurance (IA) capabilities, seamless integration with Product Lifecycle Management (PLM) environments, and effective mechanisms for secure data exchange across operational networks. This limitation not only hinders data integrity and configuration control but also increases vulnerabilities to cyber threats, jeopardizing mission-critical operations. The rapid pace of platform evolution and the increasing reliance on Model-Based Definition (MBD) and digital twin technologies further exacerbate the need for a comprehensive solution that ensures TDP security, scalability, and operational readiness.

Opportunity and Desired Outcome:

This Directed to Phase II (D2P2) SBIR effort aims to develop an innovative, scalable, and secure solution to modernize TDPs to support the lifecycle of highly complex Air and Space Force platforms. The envisioned solution will integrate advanced IA protocols, cryptographic protections, and tools for encrypted data exchange to facilitate the secure management of the "as-sustained" configuration state of critical assets. The outcome will be a functional prototype capable of enabling secure TDP lifecycle management while aligning with the Trusted AI and Autonomy modernization priorities and Zero Trust Architecture principles. The proposed solution will enhance operational efficiency, minimize cyber risks, and establish a foundation for scalable implementation across DoD platforms.

The project’s Technology Readiness Level (TRL) at the start is anticipated to be TRL 4, with the target of reaching a minimum TRL 6 by the conclusion of Phase II, including validation of core capabilities in a relevant operational environment.

Required Efforts and Phase Activities:

To achieve the stated objectives, the following efforts and activities are required for each phase of the project:

Phase II:

Develop a secure visualization tool for displaying large-scale MBD geometry and associated data through encrypted web-based interfaces.

Implement an encrypted configuration management system to maintain and update the "as-sustained" asset state while ensuring strict data integrity.

Create advanced tools for automated data quality checks, incorporating rules-based IA compliance validation to ensure all TDPs meet security and contractual requirements.

Design an end-to-end encrypted exchange framework for TDPs, incorporating user authentication, authorization, and audit trails while conforming to DoD Zero Trust Architecture guidelines.

Integrate AI/ML methodologies to enable secure damage detection, sustainment planning, and actionable insights into asset health.

Demonstrate the prototype in an operationally relevant environment, proving feasibility, security compliance, and system performance in handling large and diverse data streams.

Minimum Deliverables:

A secure web-based MBD visualization prototype capable of rendering large-scale geometry and TDP datasets with sub-second response times and role-based access controls.

Tools for encrypted configuration management and secure "as-sustained" state maintenance, integrated with PLM systems.

An automated framework for data quality checks and IA compliance validation of TDPs using defined security protocols and rules-based engines.

A cryptographic data transfer and exchange framework, with test results demonstrating alignment with DoD security policies and successful inter-organizational data exchange.

Technical documentation detailing methodologies, system architecture, and IA protocols implemented during the project, including recommendations for further scaling and operationalization.

A transition plan for integrating the developed TDP modernization technology into operational environments within the Air and Space Force platforms, supported by a detailed commercialization strategy aligned with mission needs.

Significance and Contribution to DoD Objectives:

The proposed solution directly addresses the Operational Imperative 7—Readiness to Deploy and Fight—by delivering secure and reliable tools for managing critical asset data. The project also supports the DoD’s Trusted AI and Autonomy priorities by incorporating advanced data protection mechanisms, secure autonomous processes, and scalable solutions for data management across platforms. Successful execution of this effort will enhance the DoD’s ability to maintain readiness, ensure data security, and streamline collaboration with stakeholders while safeguarding sensitive information in a rapidly evolving threat landscape.

Phase I:
As this is a Direct-to-Phase-II (D2P2) topic, no Phase I awards will be made. Offerors must demonstrate completion of Phase I feasibility research and development that is not based upon or logically extend from any prior or ongoing federally funded SBIR or STTR work, demonstrating clear technical merit, alignment with Trusted AI/Autonomy priorities, and DoD Zero Trust standards, such as validated data, performance metrics, technical reports, prototype success, or demonstrated capabilities in relevant operational environments.

Phase II:
The Phase II effort will deliver a secure, scalable prototype for modernizing Technical Data Packages (TDPs). Focus areas include encrypted configuration management, MBD visualization tools, automated IA compliance frameworks, and secure data exchange via Zero Trust Architecture. The solution will achieve TRL 6 with validated performance in operational environments, aiding readiness and alignment with Trusted AI and Autonomy priorities.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
The Phase III effort will advance the secure TDP modernization prototype to TRL 8, employing non-SBIR funds to integrate with Air and Space Force systems. Military applications include secure lifecycle management of technical data for advanced platforms, enhancing readiness and cybersecurity. Commercial use spans aerospace, manufacturing, and defense industries for data security and configuration management. Transition efforts target expanded adoption within DoD and allied partners.

title: US Production of Ultra-High Temperature Ceramic-Yielding Preceramic Polymers

description:
Objective:
The Department of the Air Force seeks to establish the domestic production of ultra-high temperature ceramic (UHTC)-yielding preceramic polymers. UHTCs are used for demanding aerospace applications, including propulsion and aeroshell components.

Description:
The scaled production of C/C-UHTCs composites (UHTCMCs) for defense applications requires the manufacturing of UHTC precursors in quantities sufficient to support acquisition programs. This SBIR will establish production of an AFRL-patented UHTC preceramic polymers so that the materials are available, at scale and affordable price point, to the high-temperature composite production community.

Phase I:
This topic is intended for technologies ready to move directly into a Phase II program. As this is a Direct-to-Phase-II (D2P2) topic, no Phase I awards will be made. Offerors must provide detailed documentation in their Direct to Phase II (D2P2) proposal that demonstrates the successful completion of a "Phase I-like" effort. This includes a feasibility study showing expertise in synthesizing and handling air/water-sensitive chemical compounds. Demonstrated experience in scaling chemical synthesis processes from the lab to pilot scale (e.g., 5-50 kg batches) is required. The feasibility study should clearly illustrate past successes in producing high-purity materials and a foundational understanding of the safety protocols necessary for handling the relevant precursors and reagents.

Phase II:
During the Phase II program, the awardee shall: 1) Establish and document a safe, robust, and scalable chemical process for the manufacturing of the AFRL-patented UHTC-bearing preceramic polymers that meets specified purity and production volume targets. 2) Conduct a thorough safety and handling analysis for all reagents, intermediates, and waste products. Production facilities must ensure safety and environmental compliance are permissible. 3) Deliver a 5x 1 kg samples of the UHTC preceramic polymer to AFRL for internal analysis, characterization, and quality verification. The offeror shall show i) for the produced polymer: NMR, elemental analysis, rheology, and ICP/MS of the produced polymer and ii) for the polymer-derived ceramic XRD, TEM/EDS, and SEM analysis, for each lot of material made. The offeror can assume a cost of $6300/kg in raw material cost if reagents, were to be purchased from commercial chemical suppliers, to produce UHTC preceramic polymers. 4) Establish and demonstrate a dedicated production capability yielding at least 50 kg per month (>600 kg per year). 5) Deliver a total of 75 kg of the qualified UHTC preceramic polymer, appropriately packaged, to the Government by the end of the Phase II effort. 6) Provide a comprehensive cost analysis and business plan for UHTC-bearing preceramic polymer production at the target scale of >1000 kg/year a target retail price of <$5000/kg, preferably <$4000/kg, identifying key supply-chain or processing factors to drive down per-kilogram costs.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:

This will involve supplying certified preceramic polymers to prime contractors and Tier 1/2 composite manufacturers supporting defense and commercial programs of record. title: Agile Wire Harness Manipulation and Installation for Unmanned Aerial Systems
summary: Develop and demonstrate a modular, agile robotic manufacturing workcell capable of autonomously routing, aligning, inserting, and verifying flexible, non-rigid wire harnesses and electrical connectors within the highly constrained physical geometries of Unmanned Aerial Systems (UAS) and advanced munitions.
description:
Objective:
Develop and demonstrate a modular, agile robotic manufacturing workcell capable of autonomously routing, aligning, inserting, and verifying flexible, non-rigid wire harnesses and electrical connectors within the highly constrained physical geometries of Unmanned Aerial Systems (UAS) and advanced munitions.

As a Direct-to-Phase-II (D2P2) topic, the immediate goal is to transition a validated proof-of-concept software and mechanical baseline (Technology Readiness Level 4) into fully integrated, operationally viable production workcells evaluated at defense prime contractor manufacturing sites. The system must eliminate the need for hard-tooled, single-product automation by delivering an agile platform that integrates deterministic planning models with real-time, adaptive online sensory feedback. This enables the robot to navigate the unpredictable, non-rigid deformation behaviors of flexible cabling, achieve sub-millimeter positioning tolerances, and safely execute intricate "blind-mate" connection sequences within tight bulkhead quarters without manual intervention.

To support a dynamic, high-mix/low-volume defense production environment, the workcell must be designed for rapid retaskability. Offerors must demonstrate a system architecture that allows shop-floor operators to completely retask the workcell to handle an entirely different munitions or UAS harness family within a single eight-hour shift. Furthermore, the platform must establish the first end-to-end digital thread for harness operations, generating machine-readable traceability records for every routing, tensioning, and insertion step to prevent latent defects and ensure 100% military standard compliance.

The ultimate phase outcome must demonstrate a two-to-four-times cycle time improvement over legacy manual wiring techniques and a reduction in skilled labor hours per unit by at least 50%. This will directly remove the primary assembly bottleneck constraining the scale-up, surge capacity, and high-rate production of critical defense systems.

Description:
Context & BackgroundModern Department of Defense (DoD) manufacturing and depot sustainment environments increasingly depend on agile automation to scale up production and maintain rapid operational readiness. While automated assembly technologies have matured substantially for rigid components with predictable geometries, the handling of flexible materials remains a persistent challenge. Specifically, wire harness routing, connector inspection, and insertion operations are ubiquitous across the production lines of Unmanned Aerial Systems (UAS), advanced munitions families, and autonomous collaborative platforms. Currently, these intricate electrical assembly processes represent a bottleneck in UAS assembly operations. Assembly technicians must manually route non-rigid cables through confined structural cavities and execute high-precision connection steps under high-mix, low-volume production conditions. Traditional industrial robotics break down when tasked with these operations because flexible wiring deforms unpredictably during manipulation, completely violating the rigid-part assumptions and fixed, hard-tooled rules of standard automation. Problem, Opportunity, & Unmet Need The complete reliance on manual wire harness installation creates a critical capability deficiency that severely penalizes DoD manufacturing agility and surge capacity. Manual operations are fundamentally non-scalable, meaning production lines cannot dynamically "ramp-to-rate" to meet sudden spikes in theater demand. Furthermore, manual wire routing and insertion introduce human-induced variability, resulting in unquantifiable defects such as partially seated connectors, overstressed wires, or compromised bend radii. These latent defects frequently slip past standard visual inspections and surface as catastrophic electrical or communication failures during critical mission times. Aerospace prime contractors and program offices have identified this manual chokepoint as the largest automation gap in UAS and munitions production. This deficiency creates a major opportunity to implement a flexible automation solution. Resolving this challenge requires a modular, adaptive robotic workcell that handles deformable materials, operates with high positional accuracy in restricted footprints, and can be rapidly retasked between completely different product designs within a single factory shift. Desired Outcome & Technological Improvement The desired outcome of this research and development effort is a fully integrated, single-arm modular robotic manufacturing workcell capable of autonomously handling the core manipulation and installation scenarios for flexible UAS and munitions wiring harnesses. Shifting the technology from manual assembly to adaptive, sensor-driven automation will fundamentally advance the DoD technological state of the art by achieving the following targeted improvements: Deformable Material Control: The platform will combine deterministic offline path planning with adaptive, real-time online sensory feedback (such as tactile, force-torque, and vision monitoring). This closed-loop configuration enables "search and settle" machine behaviors to dynamically correct for micro-misalignments and part variability on the fly. Sub-Millimeter Tolerances: The workcell will successfully execute precise connector insertion and blind-mate assembly steps within tightly constrained geometries to a targeted positioning tolerance of $\le$ 0.5 mm.Rapid Retaskability: The system will break the paradigm of dedicated single-product manufacturing by allowing shop-floor operators to ingest new geometric data and completely retask the workcell to a novel harness family in less than 8 hours.End-to-End Digital Thread: The workcell will generate machine-readable traceability records of every insertion force profile and routing path. This delivers a reliable data audit trail to eliminate quality escapes and predict latent field defects before they manifest in flight.Minimum Acceptable DeliverablesThe following deliverables must be successfully turned over to the government to satisfy the performance requirements of this solicitation:Integrated Single-Arm Robotic Workcell: One fully functional, operational modular automation cell comprising a COTS collaborative arm manipulator, reconfigurable mounting base, interchangeable end-effectors, integrated real-time compute block, and the complete multi-modal sensor stack (vision, tactile, and force-torque instrumentation). Autonomous Software Stack & Executables: Full, unencumbered delivery of the native software architecture, including the offline CAD data-ingestion pipeline, real-time adaptive control algorithms, and localized vision-tactile tracking scripts, along with complete integration documentation.Cross-Program Retasking Report: A documented technical package demonstrating the step-by-step procedures, software tools, and data workflows used to successfully transition the physical workcell between two distinct harness families in less than 8 hours.Comprehensive Technical Data Package (TDP): System layout schematics, wiring diagrams, universal end-effector interface control documents, operational manuals, and interface guides for MES/ERP factory network synchronization. Final Performance & Verification Report: A verified engineering data package from the live prime facility demonstration detailing empirical success metrics. This must validate insertion position accuracy ($\le$ 0.5 mm), insertion force variance curves, production cycle time gains ($\ge$ 2x throughput), labor hour compression ($\ge$ 50%), and a sample data pull of the machine-readable digital thread registry.

Phase I:
As this is a Direct-to-Phase-II (D2P2) topic, no Phase I awards will be made as a result of this topic. To qualify for this D2P2 topic, Offerors must demonstrate completion of Phase I feasibility research and development that is not based upon or logically extend from any prior or ongoing federally funded SBIR or STTR work. Applicant(s) should provide documentation demonstrating a clear understanding of the mechanical handling of flexible materials, single-arm robotic kinematics, deterministic offline tool-path planning, hybrid position/force control loops, multi-modal sensor fusion (vision, force-torque, and tactile feedback), and the implementation of a machine-readable digital thread within restricted weapon and unmanned system assembly architectures.

Phase I Feasibility Context & Technical Goals

For the context of this technology's lifecycle, a traditional Phase I feasibility study represents a focused research and development effort to demonstrate the scientific, technical, and commercial merit of an automated single-arm robotic solution for non-rigid material manipulation. A successful Phase I Period of Performance establishes a baseline across the following specified technical goals, operating parameters, and functional requirements:

Deformable Material Kinematics: Analytical and simulation validation proving that a single collaborative robotic manipulator arm can grasp, lift, and maneuver flexible wire harnesses without causing structural damage, violating minimum bend radii, or exceeding maximum cable strain limits. Confined Space Operating Parameters: System modeling showing the capacity for a robotic arm to navigate and thread cabling through tight apertures and restricted structural bulkheads typical of unmanned aerial systems and compact missile fuselages. Closed-Loop Alignment Logic: Verification of multi-modal tracking logic that utilizes localized computer vision and tactile feedback to continuously calculate micro-adjustments, allowing the arm to align electrical connectors under dynamic part deformation. Compliant Mating Force Boundaries: Formulation of hybrid position/force control profiles that maintain sub-millimeter insertion accuracy while monitoring force thresholds to detect pin engagement and prevent over-force structural damage. Traceable Digital Logging: Drafting a localized data logging schema capable of recording physical insertion forces, path coordinates, and connector seating confirmations to create an immutable digital thread registry.

Successful completion of these Phase I parameters provides a clear, quantitative understanding of the underlying physics and control logic governing non-rigid material manipulation, proving the system is ready for immediate physical hardware-in-the-loop integration.

Required Feasibility Documentation for D2P2 Qualification

To bypass a traditional Phase I award and qualify for this Direct-to-Phase-II pathway, applicants must submit robust, empirical Feasibility Documentation within their proposal. This package serves as the technical justification proving the small business's technology has already retired early-stage conceptual risk and rests at an acceptable maturity level (Minimum Technology Readiness Level 4).

The following documentation types are considered sufficient to substantiate proposal feasibility and must be explicitly provided:

• Empirical Performance Reports and Laboratory Data

Applicants must submit formal engineering reports, test logs, software execution records, or laboratory datasets detailing the execution of prior automated material insertion or routing. This documentation should highlight successful testing of collaborative robotic systems manipulating flexible parts. Data must explicitly demonstrate that the applicant has previously developed software or hardware-in-the-loop scripts capable of driving multi-axis trajectories to grip and move non-rigid items dynamically.

• Cross-Program Proof-of-Concept Benchmarks

Sufficient documentation includes technical summaries, contract performance reviews, or closeout reports from prior non-SBIR federal, academic, or internally funded manufacturing R&D efforts. Specifically, applicants can substantiate feasibility by detailing successful milestones from past automated flexible-assembly initiatives, such as:

Documented integration of robotic platforms optimized for compliant, multi-modal material tracking (e.g., past project outcomes managed under Advanced Robotics for Manufacturing Institute programs).Validated operational results from previous laboratory validation campaigns focused on flexible component manipulation, demonstrating early-stage handling of part deformation and configuration variability.

• Prototype Success Criteria and Interface Control Documents

Applicants must provide evidence of an existing physical or digital prototype. The documentation must exhibit a functional architecture of a single-arm cell, demonstrating how the software handles geometric inputs to calculate tool paths. Success criteria of the prior prototype must demonstrate that the hardware and software configuration can successfully manage flexible materials under variable lighting or workspace clutter, establishing a stable, cloud-independent edge-computing loop prepared for live factory scaling.

By compiling these specific reports, datasets, and mechanical baselines, the applicant provides the Air Force with clear evidence that the foundational technological risks have been thoroughly retired. This proves the single-arm architecture is mature, viable, and prepared to immediately enter the accelerated Phase II prototype integration, laboratory workcell validation, and live TRL 7 pilot production testing schedule.

Phase II:
The Phase II period of performance represents a substantial research, development, and hardware-software integration effort. It transitions the single-arm robotic technology from a validated laboratory concept into an operationally viable, modular manufacturing prototype ready for deployment on active aerospace production lines. To establish a clear, unambiguous standard for project success, the following functional requirements, operating parameters, testing regimens, and quantitative milestones are defined as the mandatory baseline for the Phase II effort.1. Functional Requirements & Technical GoalsThe Phase II effort must deliver a fully integrated, single-arm modular robotic manufacturing workcell that achieves the following technical benchmarks:Hardware-Agnostic Core Integration: Physical integration of a single collaborative manipulator arm mounted onto a reconfigurable or mobile mounting base. The control layer and sensory infrastructure must remain entirely program-agnostic, allowing the system to adapt to different vendor components without requiring a structural mechanical redesign.Autonomous Ingestion & Macro Planning: An offline planning engine capable of ingesting 3D CAD models, engineering metadata, and raw wire harness specifications. This engine must automatically produce verifiable, macro-approach robot trajectories and cable-routing path plans that strictly respect part geometry, cable bend radii, and strain limits.Adaptive Online Control Loop: A native, low-latency software control stack that runs in real-time on local hardware without cloud dependency. The system must utilize real-time tactile, force-torque, and vision feedback to dynamically adjust joint positions and execute compliant connector mating.Human-Like "Search and Settle" Behavior: Integration of hybrid position/force control mechanisms. The single arm must actively use force-torque feedback to perform search-and-settle sub-millimeter corrections during blind-mate insertion sequences where direct visual confirmation is obscured or impossible.Machine-Readable Traceability (Digital Thread): The workcell must implement the first end-to-end digital thread registry for harness assembly operations. The software must automatically log machine-readable records of every cable insertion force profile, routing coordinate, and connection seating confirmation to eliminate quality escapes and prevent latent field failures.2. Operating Parameters & Use CasesThe integrated single-arm automation system must operate reliably within the following boundaries:Physical Footprint & Access Clearance: The complete robotic tool head and manipulator assembly must be engineered to operate within the highly constrained physical envelopes and narrow clearance tracks of defensive aircraft and munitions architectures.Part Deformation Management: The system must dynamically adapt to non-rigid part behavior, actively compensating for the unpredictable bending, flexing, and micro-variability introduced during manual pre-assembly or technician handling.Primary Mission Use Case (Single-Arm Munitions Wiring): The primary operational use case involves deploying the modular workcell to automate the core wiring and electrical routing steps for complex defense systems—including the Franklin Affordable Mass Missile (FAMM) and Coyote Missile families. The system must execute aperture threading, vision/tactile-guided connector alignment, force-compliant insertion, and connection verification on representative aerospace hardware.Achieving the above should deliver a fully validated, production-ready manufacturing technology that drops labor constraints, provides comprehensive digital quality data, and dramatically scales the industrial surge capacity required for Great Power Competition.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
The contractor will pursue commercialization of the technology, targeting government program offices, commercial industrial base stakeholders. and dual use industrial customers.

The technology within this topic is restricted under the International Traffic in Arms Regulation (ITAR), 22 CFR Parts 120-130, which controls the export and import of defense-related material and services, including export of sensitive technical data, or the Export Administration Regulation (EAR), 15 CFR Parts 730-774, which controls dual use items. Develop and demonstrate an automated, end-to-end software platform capable of ingesting heterogeneous Technical Data Packages (TDPs)—including 3D CAD models, 2D engineering drawings, Bills of Materials (BOMs), and textual specifications—to autonomously extract engineering intent and generate optimized, collision-free robotic inspection trajectories without manual waypoint programming or hard-coded scripting.The resulting system must bridge the gap between enterprise digital design data and physical automation by converting complex tolerances, geometric constraints, and manufacturing annotations into a standardized data model, simulating the execution virtually, and deploying executable inspection commands directly to physical mobile robotic manipulators. (Design and fabrication of the physical manipulator is not within scope - this project will focus on translating TDPs to robot-ingestible task specification and pathing.) The objective is to drastically compress quality control programming timelines from days to under two hours and enable rapid robotic reconfiguration in highly agile manufacturing environments.

Description:
Here is a draft for a Direct to Phase II SBIR solicitation topic based on the technical capabilities of the data extraction and automated path-planning pipeline. The content has been carefully structured to be precise and concise while protecting all proprietary text.Direct to Phase II Topic DraftTopic ObjectiveObjective: Develop and demonstrate an automated, end-to-end software platform capable of ingesting heterogeneous Technical Data Packages (TDPs)—including 3D CAD models, 2D engineering drawings, Bills of Materials (BOMs), and textual specifications—to autonomously extract engineering intent and generate optimized, collision-free robotic inspection trajectories without manual waypoint programming or hard-coded scripting.The resulting system must bridge the gap between enterprise digital design data and physical automation by converting complex tolerances, geometric constraints, and manufacturing annotations into a standardized data model, simulating the execution in a physics-accurate virtual sandbox, and deploying executable inspection commands directly to physical mobile robotic manipulators. The objective is to drastically compress quality control programming timelines from days to under two hours and enable rapid robotic reconfiguration in highly agile manufacturing environments.Topic DescriptionBackground & Problem Statement: Modern aerospace manufacturing and sustainment pipelines face severe bottlenecks due to legacy quality control (QC) practices. As defense systems shift toward highly modular, rapidly evolving, and low-cost attritable architectures, traditional fixed automation becomes commercially and operationally impractical. Traditional robotic inspection lines require highly specialized programmers to manually teach waypoints, configure physical sensor triggers, and execute tedious trial-and-error collision testing on vendor-specific offline programming utilities. This labor-intensive paradigm introduces severe production delays, as errors or dimensional variations are often caught late in the assembly stream, resulting in compounding downstream costs and extended lead times.While digital enterprise structures routinely house complete engineering intent within comprehensive Technical Data Packages (TDPs)—complete with 3D geometry, Geometric Dimensioning and Tolerancing (GD&T) markers, material specifications, and assembly metadata—translating this multi-format data into actionable instructions remains a manual and error-prone process. To meet the demand for rapid production scaling and point-of-need deployment, the Department of the Air Force requires an intelligent software layer that dynamically parses TDP data and translates it directly into autonomous robotic execution paths.Phase II Expected Outcomes: Proposers responding to this Direct to Phase II topic must demonstrate a mature conceptual foundation, such as completed preliminary software blocks or data-parsing prototypes originally validated under related early-stage research. Phase II efforts must deliver a hardened, end-to-end software prototype validated against representative aerospace assembly geometries.Key technical deliverables include the ingestion/planning software, documentation for enterprise data interfaces, and localized simulation proof-of-concepts. The system performance will be benchmarked against key parameters, targeting a setup time reduction to under 8 hours for novel manufacturing configurations and compressing numerical programming timelines down to less than 1.5 hours. Final validation should culminate in a software-driven execution demo using either high-fidelity simulations or physical manufacturing hardware within a pilot production framework.

Phase I:
As this is a Direct-to-Phase-II (D2P2) topic, no Phase I awards will be made as a result of this topic. To qualify for this D2P2 topic, Offerors must demonstrate completion of Phase I feasibility research and development that is not based upon or logically extend from any prior or ongoing federally funded SBIR or STTR work. Applicant(s) should provide documentation demonstrating a clear understanding of the technical challenges associated with processing enterprise data, extracting design intent, and validating automated path execution.

The purpose of this Feasibility Documentation is to substantiate that the small business's technology is currently at an acceptable maturity level to immediately execute the prototype development, testing, and system integration required in Phase II.

Required Substantiation Components

Offerors must submit a structured technical package within the proposal (typically matching the Department of Defense Volume 2 Technical Guidance) that clearly defines the current technological baseline. Offerors must explicitly demonstrate that they possess the intellectual property rights or native ownership of the algorithmic baselines being brought forward. This foundational proof cannot be purely conceptual or marketing-driven; it must contain raw technical and analytical validation.

To satisfy the specific constraints of an automated enterprise-data-to-robotic-execution pipeline, the documentation must provide evidence across three core domains:

Ingestion & Semantic Interpretation Capability: Documentation showing the mature capability of existing code blocks or analytical tools to ingest engineering files (such as 3D CAD models, STEP files, or legacy 2D PDFs) and systematically isolate geometric structures, dimensional annotations, and textual production notes. Standardized Data Architecture: Evidence of a functional relational schema, database template, or centralized data graph structure utilized by the software to catalog and bind extracted dimensions directly to spatial CAD nodes. Kinematic & Simulation Mechanics: Proof that the small business has successfully compiled algorithms capable of reading logical manufacturing sequences and converting them into multi-axis spatial motions or automated path-planning trajectories within a virtual modeling sandbox.

Acceptable Forms of Evidence

The Air Force will evaluate the proposal based on empirical data rather than speculative milestones. Offerors should supply a combination of the following documentation types to conclusively prove feasibility:

Technical Reports and White Papers: Comprehensive white papers detailing the results, architectural limitations, and developmental conclusions of previous internally funded research or non-SBIR commercial software deployments. These reports must highlight how previous iterations successfully managed multi-format document exceptions. Empirical Test and Measurement Data: Quantitative performance charts indicating the precision and accuracy of the software's semantic parsing or extraction engines. This includes specific metrics on Optical Character Recognition (OCR) error rates, geometric normalization latency, or vector parsing precision. Prototype Design Schematics and Software Architecture Models: Logic flow charts, structural class diagrams, API data contract definitions, and interface maps illustrating how data progresses from raw enterprise packages into a centralized repository, and ultimately into automated motion commands. Simulation Benchmarks and Run-Time Measurements: Time-study records, compute logs, or comparative tables tracking the computational time required to automatically generate path trajectories relative to manual offline programming configurations. This data should ideally record baseline path-generation cycle times to validate the scaling potential of the optimization engine. Defined Prototype Success Criteria: Clear operational boundaries, algorithmic tolerances, and pass/fail thresholds under which previous internal iterations achieved successful outcomes. Offerors must list the specific file sizes, component geometric complexities, and degree of nesting variations that their software baseline has successfully parsed without human intervention.

Failure to provide rigorous, quantitative proof of a functioning software baseline that bridges data ingestion with basic path computation will result in a determination of technical non-conformance, rendering the proposal ineligible for a Direct-to-Phase-II award.

Phase II:
Phase II Expected Outcomes and Technical Framework The Phase II effort represents a major research, development, and engineering push aimed at transitioning the foundational software baseline into a hardened, production-ready enterprise platform. The overarching objective is to eliminate the manual overhead, human parsing errors, and rigid programming loops that bottleneck modern aerospace manufacturing lines. By the conclusion of the Period of Performance, the recipient must deliver a mature, well-defined software ecosystem capable of directly translating raw engineering intent into optimized, collision-free multi-axis robotic paths. The final system must demonstrate operational viability and full structural traceability back to the originating digital assets.Operating Parameters & Use Cases The software suite must maintain operational viability across highly dynamic industrial settings. Phase II development must satisfy the following baseline parameters and specific deployment use cases: Ingestion of Heterogeneous Artifacts: The ingestion system must process and map multi-vendor file formats natively without relying on manual pre-formatting or external template modifications. This includes parsing geometric data types (e.g., STEP, IGES) alongside flat text and visual annotations (e.g., drawings, PDF specification sheets, text-based process blocks).Use Case 1: Rapid Line Reconfiguration: The primary manufacturing usecase is the rapid setup of robotic tasks for modular or short-run components, specifically targeting complex structure profiles typical of autonomous collaborative platforms (ACPs) or unmanned aircraft structures. Use Case 2: Multi-Vendor Kinematic Adaptation: The trajectory engine must adapt logical tasks to varied multi-axis robotic hardware platforms (e.g., varied serial arms paired with mobile transport carts or tracked bases). The software must abstract the path calculations from specific OEM programming semantics, allowing uniform execution across distinct vendor controllers. Technical Goals & Functional Requirements The software platform must be architected as a modular, cohesive system organized across clear functional layers: Engineering Intent Processing and Graphing: The system must isolate complex design specifications—such as Geometric Dimensioning and Tolerancing (GD&T) callouts, fastener tolerances, and localized surface processing sequences—from raw documents and compile them into a relational schema or centralized data architecture. This framework must programmatically bind quantitative quality boundaries directly to the respective spatial locations on the 3D target geometry. Autonomous Path & Sequence Generation: Using the compiled structural schema, the planning block must calculate the sequence of activities independently. It must automatically optimize physical tracking angles, sensor stand-off distances, and surface normal orientations without traditional waypoint scripting or manual joystick teaching. No-Code Operator Interface: To support floor personnel who lack advanced programming backgrounds, the platform must include an intuitive, no-code graphical layer. This dashboard must visually highlight the automatically derived inspection points, outline the planned tool paths, and provide a human-in-the-loop review portal to allow manual modifications or explicit process validation before runtime deployment. The culmination of this project will be a software platform has reached a Technology Readiness Level (TRL) of 6/7, fully capable of driving multi-vendor industrial manipulators directly from enterprise data packages.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
The contractor will pursue commercialization of the technology, targeting government program offices, commercial industrial base stakeholders. and dual use industrial customers.

Develop and demonstrate advanced power source technologies capable of meeting weapon requirements with specific energy and power equal to or greater than current reserve battery technologies.

Description:
Power source performance in terms of power and energy density is the major objective with affordability, safety, and reliability secondary objectives of Air Force Armament Directorate programs for advanced reserve power sources for weapon systems. Secondary objectives are not distant relative to the major objective, but power and energy density is emphasized in order to enable new concepts and integration strategies. Current reserve thermally activated battery technology is at risk of becoming obsolete due to increasing specific power and specific energy requirements, while other battery technologies with similar or greater specific energy suffer from multiple failure modes, have limited storage life, or have not been tailored to meet the unique requirements for Air Force weapon programs. An advanced reserve power source lasting 20+ years without the need for maintenance or significant energy loss while in storage, is reliable, and is inherently safe, e.g. is not susceptible to thermal runaway, is required. Weapons typically have storage lifetimes of 20+ years; and must maintain reliable operation at any point within this time period without the power source being inadvertently activated. When the power source is activated, it must rise to full voltage within 600 ms and have an activated life of 5+ minutes. The power source must be able to survive shock, vibration, and temperatures (MIL-HDBK-310 1% Hot/ 1% Cold Days, worldwide) associated with external and internal carriage, high speed free flight, and storage environments. The power source will be required to provide power for weapon avionics, guidance, and ordnance initiation events for the entire flight profile. The load on the power source must be capable of periods of pulse power with an average 2.5 kW/kg minimum and a goal to exceed 5 kW/kg load over 60 seconds. The goal of this technology development is to design, develop, and test an advanced design for a power source capable of 20+ years of storage, 5+ minutes of activated life, with a specific energy at a minimum of 40 Wh/kg and a goal to exceed 100 Wh/kg. The power source must be inherently safe during its entire lifetime. Due to the safety issues associated with lithium battery technologies and the process to receive certification through the Naval Ordnance Security and Safety Activity (NOSSA) for use on an ordnance system, lithium battery technologies will need to demonstrate no venting under NAVSEA S9310-AQ-SAF-010 test conditions.

Prior efforts used to demonstrate feasibility must identify candidate materials, technologies and designs including the rationale for being acceptable in addition to performance data.

Phase II:
Conduct performance testing to establish design performance characteristics (Wh/kg, Wh/L, temperature range, power capability) and safety. Upon selection government provided data may be used to develop prototype designs. The deliverables for this phase consist of: 1) Prototype power source delivering 2.5 kW/kg for 60 seconds. 2) Performance characterization through testing to include captive carry and free flight shock and vibration : a. Wh/kg, b. Wh/L, c. power capability, d. temperature range, e. safety characterization.3) A manufacturing assessment of a concept design.

title: Shallow Jet Spurt Engineering Model
summary: Create a physics-based engineering model solution for shallow fuel jet spurts
description:
Objective:
Create a physics-based engineering model solution for shallow fuel jet spurts

Description:
This topic seeks the development of a computationally efficient engineering-level model to predict the formation and characteristics of the "spurt" in fluid cavity created jets. The hydrodynamic spurt is the initial, often unsteady, ejection of material from the liner, preceding the formation of the main, stable jet. Current hydrocodes can model this phenomenon but are computationally expensive and ill-suited for rapid design iteration. This project will develop a validated, reduced-order model that accurately predicts spurt velocity, mass, and geometry as a function of liner material, geometry, and threat characteristics, enabling faster design and optimization of advanced warheads.

Phase I:
Identify and analyze the key physical mechanisms governing spurt formation using existing literature and high-fidelity hydrocode simulation- Identify and analyze the key physical mechanisms governing spurt formation using existing literature and high-fidelity hydrocode simulations. Develop a preliminary analytical or semi-empirical framework for the model. Demonstrate the feasibility of the proposed model to predict spurt characteristics for a baseline test case. Develop a preliminary analytical or semi-empirical framework for the model. Demonstrate the feasibility of the proposed model to predict spurt characteristics for a baseline shaped charge design. The final report detailing the model's theoretical basis and demonstrating a proof-of-concept correlation with high-fidelity simulation data for at least one configuration.

Phase II:
Develop the engineering model into a robust software prototype. Expand the model to account for a wider range of liner materials, geometries, and explosive types. Conduct extensive validation of the model against a matrix of existing or newly generated experimental data. A validated software tool capable of predicting spurt parameters with a defined level of accuracy. The tool should be significantly faster (orders of magnitude) than full hydrocode runs.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
Harden the software for integration into the DoD's standard warhead design toolchains. Provide training and support to government and prime contractor engineering teams. title: Optimally Packaged Assembly for Laser Systems (OPALS)
summary: High-energy lasers integrated onto airborne platforms hold immense potential for a variety of applications, relevant to DAF missions.
description:
Objective:
High-energy lasers integrated onto airborne platforms hold immense potential for a variety of applications, relevant to DAF missions. However, the demanding operational environments encountered by airborne systems, characterized by factors like vibration, shock, temperature fluctuations, and pressure variations, pose significant challenges to the performance and reliability of traditional optical systems. To achieve demanding pointing and line of sight stabilization requirements necessary for the laser to have the desired effect on target, a precision optical beam control system is required to sense and correct platform induced disturbances, acquire and track targets, and sense and compensate for atmospheric and aero-optical disturbances. Historically these optical systems are implemented on flat optical benches or breadboards, in a similar manner to a ground-based laboratory. To fully realize the potential of airborne laser systems, there is a critical need for innovative optical systems designed specifically for ruggedness and environmental stability. This research effort aims to develop and demonstrate a ruggedized, environmentally stable, and optimally packaged optical beam control system specifically tailored for airborne high-energy laser applications, in a more optimized form factor for an airborne system than a conventional flat optical bench or breadboard.

Description:
The Air Force requires light weight, compactly packaged optical systems to perform critical beam control functions for airborne high energy laser systems. The purpose of this topic is not to develop new outer moldlines or turret designs for airborne systems but rather focus on optimizing the packaging and performance of the internal optical system required to perform the core beam control functions. A canonical layout of such system is available in Reference 1. The Government expects the designed beam control system will perform all functions laid out in the canonical design - or that any deviations are thoroughly understood and technically justified. Additionally, designs should prioritize ease of alignment and component replacement, potential for line replaceable units, beam path conditioning, and material free of shedding contaminants which could lead to foreign object damage. In order to achieve these objectives, the Government anticipates investigations into the following areas, although this list is informational and is intended to be neither proscriptive nor comprehensive:Ruggedized Optical Design and MaterialsRobust Packaging and Assembly TechniquesNovel Optical Architectures: Explore and develop innovative optical designs inherently tolerant to vibrations, shocks, and thermal gradients.Advanced Materials Selection: Investigate and characterize advanced materials with superior thermo-mechanical properties. This includes exploring specialized glasses, ceramics, and composites for optical elements and mounting structures.Advanced Manufacturing and Assembly Processes: Investigate and implement advanced manufacturing techniques, such as additive manufacturing and precision micro-assembly, to fabricate intricate components and achieve high-precision alignment and bonding of optical elements.Athermalized Design Strategies: Implement passive and active athermalization techniques to mitigate the performance degradation caused by temperature fluctuations. This involves optimizing material choices, employing thermal compensation methods.

Phase I:
In phase I the basic concept for the beam control mounting structure will be developed and investigated. Initial performance estimates will be modeled and an initial estimate of size and weight will be calculated. The Government anticipates numerous trade studies and design excursions to create the conceptual design for the OPALS beam control subsystem. During Phase I, concepts developed should be as platform agnostic as feasible. The Government will provide platform representative vibration spectra for performance analysis. The Government anticipates the majority of the concept development to support a Phase II prototype capable of propagating an up to ~20kW laser. However, the concept should also address issues relating to the transition to the phase III operationalized system, capable of accepting a laser of at least 300kW.

Phase II:
For the Phase II, the proposals should include development, installation, integration, demonstration, test and evaluation of the proposed optimally packaged beam control prototype system. This Phase II will seek to implement and demonstrate the feasibility of the optimally packaged beam control subsystem using a government furnished laser with power <= 20 kW, for both ground and airborne laboratory tests. AFRL is developing an Airborne Laser System Integration Laboratory to perform experimentation of advanced technologies and concepts relating to airborne high energy laser systems. The first iterations of this laboratory system will have a conventionally implemented (i.e. bench based) beam control subsystem, but subsequent upgrades are planned, and if successful we anticipate demonstrating the OPALS beam control subsystem in this laboratory. AFRL will work collaboratively to define interfaces, develop requirements, and further refine performance estimates. The work done as part of this proposed effort should be applicable to reduce risk for a full-scale system design. Efforts will include:- Perform relevant modeling and simulation to facilitate system design- Design, build, and field test a ground-based demonstration beam control subsystem to collaboratively operate with AFRL laser source- Deliver the system and associated documentation to AFRL

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
Phase III will focus on scaling up the phase II prototype into an beam control subsystem for integration onto a large, operationally relevant aircraft. The developer and AFRL will work directly with a transition partner in order to incorporate the OPALS technology into a high energy laser system significantly more powerful than the prototype system - anticipated to be at least 300kW.
