title: Multiple Telemetry Site Signal Source Synchronization
summary: The objective of this project is to study, develop, test, and field a system that addresses a critical gap in pre-mission verification and validation of receive systems supporting flight test missions that transition between multiple, geographically diverse Test and Training Ranges.
description:
Objective:
The objective of this project is to study, develop, test, and field a system that addresses a critical gap in pre-mission verification and validation of receive systems supporting flight test missions that transition between multiple, geographically diverse Test and Training Ranges. The end goal is to achieve a fully operational system that enables synchronized telemetry test signals across all participating ranges. This will allow for a comprehensive, end-to-end system checkout before a live test, significantly reducing operational and data fidelity risks, enhancing test accuracy, and strengthening mission readiness for advanced DoW test scenarios.

Description:
Flight test missions that traverse multiple Test Ranges (e.g. hypersonic vehicles/weapons, cruise missiles, long-range weapon systems etc.) or that require different test support infrastructures (e.g. sea range, targets, threat simulators, etc.) at remote Test Ranges, require telemetry receive stations along the flight paths to receive real-time telemetry and then relay that data via ground networks to the control room monitoring the mission. In past mission pre-flight scenarios, remote telemetry receive site to control room links were checked individually. This was accomplished with a local bore sight signal simulator that transmitted a known test pattern at the center frequency of the actual test article. The telemetry receive site would receive the radio frequency signal, demodulate/decode it, then send the data via Internet protocol (IP) networks to the control room. In the control room the received data was verified to be correct as the bit pattern received could be compared to the bit pattern transmitted. This was accomplished for each local and remote telemetry receive site prior to the mission.During the test, each local and remote telemetry receive site would send data to the control room and a manual switch would be accomplished between each data source based on data quality that was determined manually. Note, this selection was not automated.With the invent of best source selection using data quality metrics transferred over IP networks via data quality encapsulation [1], no longer is election of multiple data sources done manually. Telemetry receivers now assess received data quality and assign a bit error probability to a packet of data prior to sending it to the best source selector in the control room. A best source selector (BSS) inputs these multiple streams, performs time alignment, then using the data quality metric, selects the best data to output on a bit-by-bit basis. This output is the best data using all available data streams from diverse receive sites.Though higher quality, near error-free data is now provided to the control room, the addition of the BSS has revealed a shortfall. The entire data path from remote receive sites to transport through best source selection to control room cannot be tested as a complete system to assess mission readiness. The traditional method of pre-flight checks cannot be used. Why? The best source selector will not be able to correlate the multiple data streams from remote sites as the signal sources will not be correlated. This results in the configuration and operation of the BSS being unknown until the test mission. The proposed work will focus on solving this shortfall resulting in a networked, synchronized telemetry validation system capable of simulating a test vehicle's telemetry signal at multiple ground stations simultaneously. Stated another way, the proposed system must simulate the test article signal as if all telemetry receive stations could “see” the test article and simultaneously receive the telemetry signal. This capability will allow test ranges to perform pre-mission verification of the entire telemetry infrastructure. This would include all participating receive antennas, distribution networks, and best source selector(s) to control room displays to ensure full system connectivity and performance before supporting a live mission.

Phase I:
Phase I should assess the scientific and technical merit and feasibility of the concept proposed for Inter-Range telemetry receive system synchronization and signal source correlation. Objectives and expectations in Phase I are as follows: Thoroughly describe the shortfall identifying all components and interfaces. Reference all appropriate standards and provide a use case(s) that clearly illustrates the shortfall.Propose an architecture that addresses and solves this shortfall. A solution should provide a solution that incorporates multiple, spatially diverse telemetry signal sources/simulators and synchronizes these sources with precise, common time and frequency reference across all sites.Derive a master-client network architecture with a centralized command and control graphical user interface. This will allow an operator to remotely configure, manage, and monitor all signal sources/simulators from a centralized location.At the core of this solution, develop a protocol that precisely aligns all remote pseudo-random bit sequences (PRBS) generated by each simulator.

Phase II:
The Phase II effort will focus on the research, development, and delivery of a prototype system. The principal objectives include:Objective 1: Telemetry Signal Synchronization: Develop a master-client protocol and integrate a timing solution to achieve time-aligned signal generation across multiple remote telemetry signal simulators.Objective 2: Command and Control: Implement a web-based graphical user interface (GUI) for centralized configuration, status monitoring, and control of all remote simulators from a single centralized interface.Objective 3: Multi-Site Telemetry Signal Source Verification and Testing: Demonstrate multi-site correlation through bit error rate (BER) testing integrating best source selection (BSS). This includes simulating real-world impairments such as network latency and jitter. This can be simulated or with actual hardware (see Objective 4).Objective 4: Lab Verification of Hardware: Demonstrate proposed hardware in a lab environment.Objective 5: In the Field Validation of Hardware: Demonstrate the prototype system, consisting of a minimum of three signal sources controlled via a central control hub. The prototype system will be installed and tested at three geographically diverse locations. For example, that can be three sites at one Range, or one site at three Ranges (e.g. Edwards AFB, China Lake Range, Pt. Mugu Sea Range).Success criteria will be based on the system's ability to achieve and maintain PRBS synchronization of the three remote signal simulators, successful execution of remote commands via the GUI, and passing multi-site BER testing at the output of the BSS.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
The Phase III effort will focus on transitioning the prototype system to a fully operational and commercially available and sustainable product. Technology is expected to enter Phase III at TRL-6 and be matured to TRL-8. Working with the Test Ranges will be key to this maturation as real-world testing will aid in process. Direct interaction with the Telemetry Group of the Range Commanders Council will ensure customer needs are integrated into the hardware as it is matured. A successful SBIR Program would result in the standardization of the end product in the Telemetry Standard IRIG-106 with adoption into the major Test Ranges.DoW Applications: The end goal for this system would be to secure procurement contracts via the SBIR Phase III pathway to deploy the end system as a standardized solution across Air Force, Army, and Navy Test Ranges. Known customer opportunities include the 412th Test Wing (Edwards AFB), 96th Test Wing (Eglin AFB), NAWCAD (Point Mugu and Patuxent River), and White Sands Missile Range as all support flight test programs that require range airspace and assets spanning multiple Ranges.Commercial Applications: Market the end system to commercial aerospace prime contractors (e.g., Boeing, Lockheed Martin) and commercial space launch providers (e.g., SpaceX, Blue Origin, ULA) to improve the efficiency and reliability of their own flight-testing programs.Business Model: The commercialization strategy will blend direct sales to DoD ranges with commercial applications.

title: Long Rod Delivery System
summary: Create a system capable of launching long rod threats with controlled angle of attack
description:
Objective:
Create a system capable of launching long rod threats with controlled angle of attack

Description:
The lack of a non-destructive, high-precision launching method for high length-to-diameter (L/D) projectiles fundamentally degrades the fidelity of Live Fire Test and Evaluation (LFT&E) data. For the Air Force, this deficiency directly compromises the development of penetrating munitions, degrades the survivability assessments of aerospace platforms, and introduces significant acquisition risks due to flawed test data and increased testing costs. Currently, there is not means of reliably controlling or manipulating the flight of a long rod projectile such that it consistently reaches a target location at a specific orientation. Providing means of accomplishing this feat advances DoW test capabilities for critical data underpinning analytical vulnerability assessments and engineering designs improving the survivability posture of current and next generation combat aircraft.

Phase I:
Conduct a comprehensive feasibility study evaluating alternative launching technologies (e.g., advanced light-gas, hybrid electromagnetic, pneumatic) against the requirement to launch high L/D ratio projectiles (1,400 m/s to >2,300 m/s) without structural degradation. Develop a conceptual design and utilize analytical modeling and simulation to predict internal ballistics, projectile acceleration curves, and exit velocities. Identify technical risks and propose mitigation strategies.

Phase II:
Execute the Phase I maturation plan by engineering, fabricating, and testing a sub-scale or full-scale prototype launching system. Conduct live-fire demonstrations using inert long-rod projectiles to validate the system's velocity range, repeatability, and precision. Integrate high-speed diagnostics (e.g., flash X-ray, high-speed imaging) to conclusively verify the structural integrity, pitch, and yaw of the projectile upon muzzle exit. Validate the system's operational viability for generating actionable LFT&E data (e.g., ballistic limit testing).

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
Transition the mature technology to government and contractor testing facilities. Integrate the launching system into major Department of War (DoW) LFT&E ranges (Army, Navy, Air Force) to support acquisition programs evaluating next-generation vehicle, aviation, and body armor. Concurrently, pursue commercialization pathways by adapting the technology for dual-use applications, such as civilian materials science research, spacecraft micrometeoroid shielding evaluation, and industrial hypervelocity impact studies.

References:

title: Luminescence-Based Surface Measurement Technique for Simultaneous Pressure and Temperature Measurements within Non-Oxygen Based Hypersonic Ground Test Facilities
summary: Develop and validate a non-intrusive, luminescence-based surface measurement technique for simultaneous pressure and temperature measurements within non-oxygen-based hypersonic ground test facilities.
description:
Objective:
Develop and validate a non-intrusive, luminescence-based surface measurement technique for simultaneous pressure and temperature measurements within non-oxygen-based hypersonic ground test facilities.

Description:
Within aerodynamic testing, pressure sensitive paint (PSP) provides crucial global surface pressure data that is utilized in calculating aerodynamic loads [1] and identifying small scale features within the flow. The working principle behind PSP involves luminophores that fluoresce at an intensity inversely proportional to the number of oxygen molecules present i.e., oxygen quenching [2].

While these paints/luminophores have been sufficiently researched, the use-case of these paints is severely limited due to the requirement of oxygen in the flow field. Advanced hypersonic wind tunnels such as the blowdown facility at AEDC Tunnel No. 9 which utilizes nitrogen as the working fluid, are unable to utilize PSP to capture global pressure data with this method and are therefore severely limited to discrete measurement techniques. It is required that a novel technique be developed to capture simultaneous global pressure and temperature measurements in nonoxygen-based hypersonic wind tunnels.

Phase I:
Phase I efforts outline technique/paint development and establish feasibility through thorough characterization of the paint properties/sensitivities and reduction process using benchtop testing and testing within small-scale (educational) supersonic/hypersonic facilities.

Phase II:
Phase II efforts outline full scale prototype demonstrations within a hypersonic test facility through either test probes or full-scale model testing on a well-known/standard test article. The completed technique and refined data reduction process will be delivered at this phase.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
The technique can be marketed for non-intrusive simultaneous pressure/temperature measurements in non-oxygen-based high-speed wind tunnels.

title: AI-Enabled Computed Vision Air-to-Air Refueling Performance Assessment and Automated Pilot Debrief System
summary: Develop, integrate, and demonstrate an artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled computed vision and human-machine interface capability that transforms aerial refueling operations from subjective, observation-based evaluation into an objective, data-driven performance assessment and adaptive training environment.
description:
Objective:
Develop, integrate, and demonstrate an artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled computed vision and human-machine interface capability that transforms aerial refueling operations from subjective, observation-based evaluation into an objective, data-driven performance assessment and adaptive training environment. The system shall leverage advanced computer vision, machine learning, and aviation (flight dynamics) analytics techniques to automatically extract operationally relevant performance metrics from aerial refueling events, quantify deviations from desired flight profiles, and generate actionable post-flight feedback to improve aircrew proficiency, reduce human-factor-driven mishaps, and enhance mission readiness.The capability shall analyze video from cameras mounted on the tanker (esp. the KC-46) to provide near-real-time post-flight reconstruction of aerial refueling engagements by correlating aircraft position, motion dynamics, refueling geometry, pilot inputs, and operational context to identify performance trends and training opportunities. The developed system shall perform automated assessment of complex aerial refueling behaviors including aircraft stability, closure rate management, alignment accuracy, control surface position, other situational awareness indicators, and adherence to established refueling procedures.The objective is to mature existing advanced AI-enabled aviation analytics into an operationally relevant post-flight “hotwash” and training capability that increases the instructional value of each aerial refueling sortie, reduces reliance on subjective human assessment, accelerates pilot proficiency development, decreases equipment damage associated with refueling deviations, and establishes a scalable foundation for future intelligent aviation training systems across Department of the Air Force and joint aviation communities.The resulting prototype shall demonstrate the ability to ingest operational aerial refueling data, autonomously generate objective performance assessments, provide intuitive visualization and debrief products, and support transition into existing aviation training, evaluation, and modernization ecosystems. Importantly, the system will also include automated security management of the video so that implementation is seamless and complies with security classification guidance.

Description:
Air-to-air refueling (AAR) is a critical Department of the Air Force and Department of the Navy capability enabling global mobility, long-range strike, combat airpower projection, and sustained aviation operations. However, aerial refueling remains one of the most technically demanding and safety-critical aviation tasks performed by aircrews. Successful execution requires precise aircraft positioning, coordinated control inputs, accurate closure rate management, continuous situational awareness, and effective crew coordination between tanker and receiver aircraft.Current aerial refueling training and post-flight assessment processes rely heavily on instructor observation, pilot self-assessment, manual video review, and subjective evaluation of performance. These approaches provide limited ability to quantitatively assess the thousands of individual performance variables that influence successful refueling operations. Existing methods do not provide pilots with objective, moment-by-moment feedback on aircraft positioning, closure rates, control inputs, deviations from desired procedures, or trends in individual performance over time.This topic seeks to develop, demonstrate, and transition an artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled computed vision capability that (post-flight) automatically analyzes aerial refueling operations and provides objective, data-driven pilot performance feedback. The desired capability will mature existing advances in autonomous aerial refueling analytics and apply them toward training, readiness, and safety improvement by transforming aerial refueling video and available aircraft performance data into actionable post-flight debrief products.The developed system shall provide an automated “hot wash” which analyzes aerial refueling events, identifies performance deviations, and generates intuitive visualizations that allow pilots and instructors to better understand execution quality and areas for improvement. The system shall reduce reliance on subjective recollection and manual review by providing objective measurements of aircraft performance throughout the refueling profile.The capability shall focus on analysis of tanker-mounted video data, such as KC-46 aerial refueling camera systems, while maintaining an architecture capable of expanding across additional tanker and receiver platforms. The vendor may pick (with Government concurrence) the first 3-5 receiver platforms to use in developing this system. Future applicability includes KC-135, C-17, all fighter receiver aircraft, naval aviation communities, autonomous aerial refueling systems, and other aviation training environments requiring advanced performance analytics.The desired solution shall leverage artificial intelligence, machine learning, computer vision, and advanced human-machine interfaces to provide capabilities including:• Automated detection and tracking of tanker (boom and hose) and receiver aircraft during aerial refueling operations.• Measurement of relative aircraft position, movement, velocity, and alignment throughout the refueling engagement.• Assessment of aircraft position within the approved refueling envelope.• Analysis of closure rates, approach vectors, aircraft stability, and deviations from nominal procedures.• Ability to correlate video with other aircraft data if/as available (e.g. telemetry, fuel transfer rate, fuel state, and pilot inputs) to evaluate performance drivers.• Generation of objective performance scores and trend analysis across multiple training events.• Creation of visual performance assessment products for receiver pilot post-flight review of their performance during refueling, including graphical overlays, heat maps, event timelines, and immersive or interactive debrief environments.• Support for instructor review, adjudication, and refinement of automated assessments during initial deployment.The system should evaluate innovative approaches for integrating automated analytics with existing or future aviation training environments, including virtual reality (VR), augmented reality (AR), mission rehearsal systems, simulator environments, or other computer-based training tools.The solution must address operational challenges associated with military aviation data, including secure processing of controlled aviation video, automated data protection, and protection of sensitive operational information. The capability should consider approaches for minimizing processing burden on operational units while enabling rapid generation of post-flight assessments.The Government seeks solutions which provide an operationally relevant prototype supporting aerial refueling training organizations. Successful completion of this effort will provide Air Force and joint aviation communities with a next-generation training and assessment capability that improves pilot proficiency, increases the training value of each refueling event, reduces equipment damage and maintenance impacts, and enhances overall mission readiness.The desired end state is an operationally demonstrated capability ready to implement for at least one type of receiver aircraft and that can support transition into existing aviation training ecosystems and provide a scalable foundation for future AI-enabled aviation performance assessment across the Department of Defense.

Phase I:
As this is a Direct-to-Phase-II (D2)2) topic, no Phase I proposals will be accepted and no Phase I awards will be made under this topic. Offerors responding to this topic shall demonstrate “Phase I-type” technical feasibility through prior research, development, laboratory validation, commercial development, or operational demonstrations performed outside of the SBIR/STTR program. The purpose of this demonstration will be for the Government to determine the feasibility of the ideas that appear to have the potential to satisfy the objectives of this topic:

The Government is seeking offerors with demonstrated experience and technical maturity equivalent to a successful Phase I effort. Proposals shall demonstrate existing capabilities, relevant past performance, or validated technologies applicable to the development of an AI-enabled aerial refueling performance assessment and automated pilot debrief capability.

Qualified offerors shall demonstrate experience in at least half of following technical areas:

• Development and application of artificial intelligence, machine learning, and computer vision algorithms for analyzing dynamic objects in video imagery.
• Processing and interpretation of high-speed motion imagery to determine object position, movement, velocity, orientation, and spatial relationships.
• Development of algorithms capable of tracking aircraft, vehicles, or other dynamic platforms in complex operational environments.
• Aviation-focused data analytics, flight performance monitoring, flight simulation, or aircrew training systems.
• Development of human-machine interfaces, virtual reality (VR), augmented reality (AR), immersive training environments, or advanced visualization tools.
• Integration of sensor data, video analytics, telemetry, or flight performance information into automated assessment systems.
• Experience handling, processing, protecting, or analyzing controlled aviation or operational data.
• Automated video processing techniques including object recognition, classification, filtering, masking, or data protection methodologies.
• Development of secure software systems capable of operating within government aviation environments.

Offerors shall demonstrate prior technical maturity equivalent to a Technology Readiness Level (TRL) 4 or greater at contract award. Relevant experience may include laboratory demonstrations, commercial applications, government-sponsored research, operational prototypes, or other non-SBIR/STTR funded development activities.

The offeror shall demonstrate the ability to transition existing technical capabilities into an operational prototype supporting aerial refueling performance analysis. Successful offerors will demonstrate sufficient technical foundation to immediately begin Phase II activities including adaptation of computer vision algorithms, integration of aviation video data, development of automated performance metrics, and operational prototype demonstration.

Evaluation of Phase I-equivalent experience will consider:

• Relevance of previous computer vision, artificial intelligence, or machine learning development efforts.
• Demonstrated ability to analyze complex motion-based systems, especially aviation maneuvers.
• Experience applying technology within aviation, aerospace, defense, and related training environments.
• Demonstrated ability to mature existing technologies into operationally relevant prototypes.
• Ability to address cybersecurity, data protection, and integration challenges associated with military aviation applications.

Phase II:
Phase II will develop, integrate, and demonstrate an operational prototype of an AI-enabled computer vision air-to-air refueling (AAR) performance assessment and automated pilot debrief system. The effort will mature existing autonomous AAR analytics into a post-flight training and evaluation capability providing objective, data-driven feedback to tanker and receiver aircrews.The prototype shall ingest AAR video and available aircraft performance data, identify deviations from desired procedures, and generate automated post-flight hotwash products. The system shall reduce reliance on pilot memory and manual instructor video review through objective measurements, visualization, and historical trend analysis.Task 1: System Architecture, Data Acquisition, and Secure ProcessingEstablish the architecture to ingest, process, analyze, and protect AAR video and associated aircraft data.Activities shall include:Develop system architecture, data flows, and cybersecurity approach.Establish procedures for CUI and operational aviation data.Integrate available tanker-mounted cameras, aircraft video, and applicable flight-performance data.Evaluate local processing with transfer of lightweight outputs versus secure video transfer to approved computing environments.Develop data-management procedures supporting expansion across tanker/receiver platforms.Deliverables: System Architecture Design; Data Management and Security Plan; CUI Processing Workflow; Initial Prototype Data Ingestion Capability.Task 2: Computer Vision Model Adaptation and Performance AnalyticsAdapt and mature existing computer vision technologies for automated AAR analysis, including aircraft motion, relative positioning, and flight-performance assessment.The capability shall:Detect/track tanker boom or hose and receiver aircraft.Determine relative position, orientation, and movement.Measure closure rates and approach vectors.Assess position within the approved refueling envelope.Identify boom, probe, or hose/drogue alignment.Analyze stability and deviations from nominal procedures.Support multiple tanker and receiver configurations.Demonstrate performance equivalent to TRL 6+ through prototype demonstration in a relevant operational environment.Deliverables: Adapted Computer Vision Models; Aircraft Tracking Algorithms; Performance Assessment Algorithms; Technical Validation Report.Task 3: Automated Performance Assessment and Pilot FeedbackConvert AAR data into objective post-flight performance feedback, including:Moment-by-moment scoring against nominal profiles.Positioning heat maps relative to the refueling envelope.Closure-rate and approach-vector analysis.Timeline reconstruction of key events.Identification of deviations/improvement areas.Historical individual and crew trend analysis.Where available, correlate performance with pilot inputs/data including fuel state/transfer rate, control inputs, throttle response, aircraft corrections, response timing, crew coordination indicators, and situational-awareness factors.To support organizational change and adjudicate corner cases, provide an instructor/"master debriefer" capability for trained personnel to review, validate, and provide feedback on automated assessments during initial deployment.Stretch Goal: Recognize, or provide a growth path to recognize, bent/broken boom, probe, or hose conditions and associated FOD.Deliverables: Automated Performance Assessment Engine; Pilot Feedback Products; Instructor Review Interface; Performance Analytics Dashboard.Task 4: Automated Data Protection and Video ProcessingDevelop secure video-processing capabilities that minimize operational burden and protect sensitive information.The system shall:Detect when a receiver aircraft is present and activate analytics only during relevant events.Identify and prevent processing/retention of unauthorized aircraft or sensitive platforms.Remove/obscure sensitive geographic information, terrain, markings, and other operationally sensitive information.Support automated masking/filtering before distribution.Demonstrate an architecture supporting future cybersecurity certification.Deliverables: Automated Video Processing Capability; Data Protection/Filtering Methodology; Cybersecurity Assessment Documentation.Task 5: Pilot Debrief Visualization and Training IntegrationDevelop intuitive visualization methods translating analytics into actionable training feedback. Evaluate/demonstrate:Immersive VR/AR replay environments.Squadron-level 2D visualization.Graphical overlays depicting aircraft position, closure rates, desired flight paths, deviations, and refueling-envelope margins.Apply instructional-design principles to support pilot learning, instructor evaluation, and squadron training discussions.Deliverables: Visualization Trade Study; Pilot Debrief Interface Prototype; Training Integration Plan.Task 6: Operational Demonstration, Testing, and TransitionDemonstrate the prototype with operational military aviation users and validate:Accuracy of automated assessments.Correlation with experienced instructor evaluations.Negligible manual video-review workload.Usability within existing training/mission-debrief workflows.Ability to generate actionable post-AAR pilot feedback.Desired Technical Performance Objectives:Generate automated debrief products within 15 minutes of video ingestion.Accurately track aircraft position, movement, and refueling geometry.Identify significant deviations from nominal procedures.Achieve ≥95% agreement between experienced instructors and automated assessments during validation.Demonstrate integration with at least one operational AAR training organization.Deliverables: Operational Prototype Demonstration; Test and Evaluation Report; User Feedback Assessment; Phase III Transition Plan.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
Phase III will support transition of the AI-enabled aerial refueling performance assessment capability into operational Air Force, Navy, USMC, and select foreign aviation communities through program office integration, operational funding pathways, and sustainment planning.Potential transition applications include:· KC-46 aerial refueling training and readiness improvement.· KC-135 and legacy tanker modernization efforts.· C-17 and other receiver aircraft training applications.· Fighter receiver aerial refueling proficiency improvement.· Navy and Marine Corps aerial refueling operations.· Autonomous aerial refueling development and validation.· Advanced aviation training and performance analytics.Commercialization opportunities may include adaptation of aviation analytics, pilot training analytics, flight performance monitoring, and simulation technologies for commercial aviation, allied aviation partners, and other safety-critical transportation environments.

References:

title: Fusion of Cooperative Information Sharing for Uncrewed Air Systems (FOCISAUS)
summary: The Department of the Air Force seeks mature, innovative solutions ready for prototype development and demonstration in cooperative perception for uncrewed or autonomous air systems.
description:
Objective:
The Department of the Air Force seeks mature, innovative solutions ready for prototype development and demonstration in cooperative perception for uncrewed or autonomous air systems. The objective of this topic is to develop and demonstrate a scalable prototype that enables distributed sensing nodes to share, prioritize, and fuse mission-relevant information in near real time to improve object detection, tracking, navigation, and operator situational awareness in cluttered and bandwidth-constrained environments.

Solutions should support efficient information exchange, adaptive transmission under changing network conditions, and a credible data fusion design that converts distributed sensor observations into actionable fused products. Offerors should propose technologies with demonstrated Phase I-type maturity and a clear path to prototype integration, testing, and transition.

Description:
Distributed air operations increasingly depend on timely awareness of objects, hazards, and activities beyond the field of view of any individual platform. Cooperative perception offers a path to extend sensing coverage and reduce blind spots by allowing multiple platforms and supporting nodes to share sensor-derived information. Yet this benefit is limited by the large size of modern sensor data, the variability of wireless links, the need for rapid decision making, and the difficulty of combining observations from different platforms, geometries, and sensing modalities.

This topic seeks prototype-ready solutions that build on prior feasibility work in distributed information sharing, compression, adaptive transmission, and sensor data fusion. The government is interested in capabilities that can select and transmit the most relevant information, manage latency and bandwidth constraints, and fuse data from multiple sources into improved perception outputs for autonomy or operator use.

Offerors should address the data fusion aspect as a core requirement of the overall solution, whether through point cloud fusion, image or radar correlation, feature or object fusion, track association, or other mission-appropriate methods. Solutions should also describe how fused outputs are exposed to mission applications, edge processing nodes, or user interfaces. Approaches that can operate under degraded or intermittent communications and can scale across multiple sensing platforms are of particular interest.

Prototype capabilities may include, but are not limited to: Distributed organization, naming, publication, discovery, or retrieval of sensor information; Adaptive data selection, fidelity control, compression, and transmission policies; Real-time or near-real-time fusion and correlation of data from multiple platforms or sensor types; Delivery of fused perception products to autonomy software, edge analytics, or mobile mission applications; and Measurable improvements in latency, bandwidth efficiency, blind-spot reduction, and detection or tracking performance.

Phase I:
This topic is intended for technologies that are sufficiently mature to proceed directly into prototype development. Therefore, Phase I awards will not be made for this topic and Phase I proposals will not be accepted. title: Cleaner for the Time Domain Reflectometer Tank Level Indicator
summary: Develop a technology to clean and potentially reverse fouling on Time Domain Reflectometer (TDR) Tank Level Indicating (TLI) components in-place. The solution must function within fully compensated fuel tanks aboard DDG 51 class ships without requiring depressurization, defueling, or dewatering.
description:
Objective:
Develop a technology to clean and potentially reverse fouling on Time Domain Reflectometer (TDR) Tank Level Indicating (TLI) components in-place. The solution must function within fully compensated fuel tanks aboard DDG 51 class ships without requiring depressurization, defueling, or dewatering.

Description:
Fouling on the TDR sensor used for TLI is a persistent problem. The TDR is necessary to provide accurate and precise readings for fuel measurement. Over time, TDRs can experience sensor fouling through a buildup of crystallization and other contaminants on TDR rods and tubes, contributing to false readings or other failures if not properly maintained and cleaned.

The operational readiness of the U.S. Navy's DDG 51 Arleigh Burke-class destroyers is being undermined by a persistent and unsolved equipment failure. The TDR sensors, a TLI technique, which are critical for managing fuel, buoyancy, and stability, are consistently rendered unreliable due to fouling. Current cleaning methods are operationally untenable; they require taking fuel compensating tanks offline, emptying fuel and/or compensating seawater, and significant follow-on maintenance, which directly reduces the Fleet's readiness and deployability. These efforts are not a permanent solution and often fail to resolve the underlying issue, making this a high-priority challenge for the DDG 51 Program Office.

The Navy urgently seeks an innovative solution that remedies fouled TDR units without requiring ships to cease operations or undergo costly, invasive maintenance, thereby increasing mission readiness and reducing the risk of fuel spills.

Effective methods for cleaning these sensors in-situ are very limited. The existing approach involves decompensation of fuel tanks (removal of fuel and compensating seawater) and manual removal of TDR sensors for cleaning, which can be costly and time consuming. It is not generally feasible while the ship is underway. Removal of TDR sensors during these manpower-intensive efforts can sometimes lead to TDR sensor miscalibration during re-installation.

The inability to effectively clean TDR sensor fouling is a critical point of failure. The buildup of crystallization and other contaminants on TDR rods and tubes creates false readings and electrical shorts, leading to inaccurate fuel measurement and extensive tracking errors. This directly compromises the precise fuel management necessary for the ship’s stability and mission readiness. Current ships have had fuel spills due to TDR TLI fouling. Additionally, scheduled maintenance periods to remove and clean fouled TDR TLI units inherently cause time delays and ship-wide disruptions affecting other planned work. .

The Navy seeks a product that cleans and potentially reverses the fouling buildup throughout the entire TDR assembly while being compatible with the existing sensor architecture. The technology must return the installed TDR and TLI technique to full operational status upon one execution of the developed technology/technique over an objective period of 36 months, but not less than a threshold period of 8 months of full TDR TLI operability. This effort is required to develop a comprehensive technique that resolves this persistent reliability challenge. A more precise fuel management and reduction in potential failures will result in greater ship stability and increased mission readiness.

Phase I:
Develop a concept for a product/technology to clean a fouled TDR TLI in-situ, returning it to full operational status within the challenging environment of a compensated fuel tank. Detail how the cleaning technology would be employed on an in-service ship while underway. Establish feasibility through small-scale testing, analysis, or modeling. If the Phase I Option is exercised, include the initial design specifications and capabilities description to build a prototype solution in a Phase II plan.

Phase II:
Develop, deliver, and demonstrate a prototype of the anti-fouling solution that meets the requirements in the Description. Prove in a demonstration that the technology can return a fouled TDR TLI to full operability in a simulated confined space without requiring the tank to be emptied or causing fuel spills. Design the solution to minimize or eliminate the need for personnel to access the tank, a key limitation of current procedures. Identify all necessary Navy testing for shipboard certification. Prepare a Phase III commercialization/transition plan.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
Support the Navy in transitioning the cleaning technology for Fleet-wide use, providing the necessary equipment, training, and logistical documentation.

A successful solution to this problem on the DDG 51 class is expected to be highly applicable to other ships facing similar challenges with compensated fuel tanks and TDR TLIs, including the LHD 1 and LHA 6 classes. The goal is to field a fully qualified and certified solution that resolves this long-standing maintenance and readiness issue across the surface fleet.

Commercial fuel tank farms as well as other industrial operations requiring high level of awareness of tank full status can benefit from development of this technology.

title: Fire Resistant Joiner Bulkhead
summary: Develop a material/system to increase the fire-resistance of joiner bulkheads on ships and compartment-level fire containment while meeting Navy requirements for weight, fit, cost, fire, smoke and toxicity.
description:
Objective:
Develop a material/system to increase the fire-resistance of joiner bulkheads on ships and compartment-level fire containment while meeting Navy requirements for weight, fit, cost, fire, smoke and toxicity.

Description:
Fire represents a grave hazard to Navy vessels. Recent fire events have propagated through joiner bulkheads and resulted in significant fire damage, which poses a substantial threat to personnel and equipment. Uncontrolled fires can propagate throughout a ship and cause extensive damage to machinery, equipment, and ship compartments; additionally, fires represent an extreme risk to ship personnel. The Navy has made numerous improvements to make ships more fire-resistant but is seeking improvement for containment of compartment-level fire events seen in recent and historical ship fires (i.e., USS OSCAR AUSTIN, USS CONYNGHAM, USS STARK, and the cruise ship Star Princess). More fire-resistant joiner bulkheads would allow damage control teams to contain and extinguish fires more easily before they could grow to threaten the ship. Innovation is needed to meet Navy goals with regard to weight, cost, fit, and performance.

The Navy seeks an improved fire-resistant joiner bulkhead that would reduce the damage ships sustain during fires, as well as improve safety for the crew.

Development of a fire-resistant joiner bulkhead faces several technical challenges. First, any fire-resistant joiner bulkhead must not have a significant weight increase. Given the quantity of joiner bulkheads onboard ships, any weight increase could add significant weight to the ships, which will impair and degrade ship performance. Second, the improved joiner bulkheads must not excessively exceed the width of current joiner bulkheads. Destroyers have confined spaces and for the comfort and operational capability of the crew, any new joiner bulkhead cannot greatly exceed the dimensions of the existing panels. Third, any fire-resistant joiner bulkhead must be a cost-effective solution for the Navy. In particular, the fire-resistant joiner bulkhead must not substantially increase the costs to install at the shipyard. The reason for this concern is that joiner bulkheads sometimes require modification at the shipyards to fit the exact dimensions of the ship. Any solution that requires expensive edge treating or would otherwise be cost-prohibitive to modify at the shipyards will not be considered. Lastly, the improved joiner bulkhead must meet or exceed the requirements to be certified for shock and fire performance as AN-30 class per MIL-STD-3020 and pass Navy Fire, Smoke, Toxicity (FST) testing per MIL-STD-1623. This is a vital requirement to demonstrate that any new material in the joiner bulkhead will not release dangerous particulates as it burns or fails if there is an impact.

Research into fire-resistant materials has revealed several technology advances in the areas of intumescent coatings, coatings that incorporate nanomaterials to aid in thermal regulation, or advanced high-performance fibers; however, there is no current commercial solution available. The Navy is also open to bio-composites, bio-polymers, or other materials that have the potential to provide superior fire-resistance with reduced toxicity as compared to many commercially available products.

Phase I:
Develop a concept for a fire-resistant joiner bulkhead that meets the requirements above. Demonstrate the feasibility of the concept in meeting the Navy needs prescribed above and establish that the concept can be developed into a useful product for the Navy. Establish feasibility of a new fire-resistant material/system via small-scale testing. If the Phase I Option is exercised, include the initial design specifications and a capabilities description to build a prototype solution in Phase II.

Phase II:
Develop and deliver a prototype fire-resistant joiner bulkhead for evaluation. (Note: The prototype will be evaluated to determine capability in meeting the performance goals defined in the Phase II SOW.) Demonstrate product performance through prototype evaluation, modeling, and demonstration over the required range of parameters as defined by the Navy. Participate in an extended evaluation in a land-based test environment to refine the prototype into a design that will meet Navy requirements. Prepare a Phase II manufacturing and development plan, including drawings of connection details, to transition the improved fire-resistant joiner bulkhead to Navy use.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
Support the Navy in transitioning the fire-resistant joiner bulkhead to Navy use. Develop installation and maintenance manuals for the improved fire-resistant joiner bulkhead to support transition to the Fleet.

Many potential commercial applications for improved fire-resistant joiner bulkheads exist; examples include commercial shipping, construction, aerospace, and automotive industries.

title: Input-Output Unit (IOU) for Secure Processing and Routing of Hull, Mechanical, & Electrical (HM&E) and Navigation Signals
summary: Develop a dust-protected, water splash-resistant Input-Output Unit (IOU) capable of interfacing with legacy and modern equipment to send, receive, process, and route signals throughout the hull and superstructure of naval vessels.
description:
Objective:
Develop a dust-protected, water splash-resistant Input-Output Unit (IOU) capable of interfacing with legacy and modern equipment to send, receive, process, and route signals throughout the hull and superstructure of naval vessels.

Description:
IOUs are used on all Navy DDG 51 class ships to transfer Steering Control, Machinery Control, and Damage Control signals, as well as Interior Communication Alarm and Indication, Synchro and Digital Navigation data. They are also used on USN LHA(R) class ships, in Aegis Ashore facilities, and across a variety of Foreign Military Sales (FMS) cases. IOUs serve as a translation point when sending and receiving non-Ethernet traffic, such as synchro and low-level serial data, to Ethernet user systems.

IOUs are installed in a variety of air-conditioned and non-air-conditioned spaces. Their use in engineering spaces that historically have relied on Halon 1301 (safe for sensitive electronics) for fire suppression has been complicated by the Navy’s transition away from Halon and toward water mist protection systems. Additionally, existing IOUs rely on the integration of a wide variety of circuit card assemblies (CCA) to process different types of signals, creating hardware challenges for lifetime support and technology refresh.

The Navy seeks to reduce lifecycle costs with a simplified design that has fewer hardware dependencies, hardware component updates, and more open and modular system architectures.

The IOU is intended to be operated continuously. The IOU shall be designed to permit routine maintenance and troubleshooting. Repair actions should be possible while the IOU is energized without loss of required functionality and operating. Reliability and Survivability are essential and all IOU components must demonstrate Mean Time Between Failures (MTBF) in excess of 10,000 hours. While the IOU as a whole product does not exist commercially, the base technology required is available in industry. The focus of this SBIR topic is to integrate the capabilities into a synergized product.

Requirements:

The Navy requires a dust-protected, water splash-resistant (IEC 60529 IP54-rated) IOU capable of interfacing with legacy and future equipment to send, receive, process, and route signals throughout the hull and superstructure of naval vessels. The enclosure must protect the power supply, cooling components, and electronics necessary to connect serial (RS-232, RS-422, RS-485, NTDS-E), fiber Ethernet, Cat 5 Ethernet (unicast, multicast), analog synchro (60 and 400 Hertz), and analog voltage (AC and DC) capabilities. External connections are made by triaxial, 42-pin, and 92-pin cables, as well as fiber optic connectors to redundant Gigabit Ethernet (GbE) shipboard networks.

Design must accommodate an additional fifty percent capacity for future growth from initial defined design specifications and capability descriptions. It must also provide adequate internal cooling while meeting or exceeding IP54 dust and spray requirements.

All hardware components must be compliant with Restriction of Hazardous Substances (RoHS) directive 2011/65/EU.

Enclosure:

Maximum size and weight (excludes external mounting dimensions):

Weight: 188 pounds; Depth: 17 inches; Width: 26 inches; Height: 27 inches.

The IOU must be mountable from the rear or the bottom and allow cable attachment/removal and reasonable access to all user interfaces and cable attachment points in any mounted configuration.

Power Supply:

Internal Alternating Current (AC) power supply will connect to two independent 120V, 60Hz shipboard lighting circuits (2 of 3 phases) for redundancy. Synchro reference power (400Hz and 60Hz) is necessary for some user interfaces (separate from IOU AC power). IOUs should require less than 600 Watts of power when fully loaded.

IOU must strictly comply with MIL-STD-1399-300, operating reliably on both Type I and Type II power. The design must tolerate all specified voltage and frequency fluctuations, withstand severe voltage spikes, and limit maximum instantaneous input current (inrush current) when initially energized. To maintain ship-wide power quality and ensure system compatibility, the IOU must also adhere to strict limits on harmonic distortion, maintain a high-power factor, and meet the electromagnetic interference (EMI) and electromagnetic compatibility (EMC) requirements of MIL-STD-461. To ensure the IOU design is suitable for shipboard environments, the IOU must meet the requirements of the latest revisions of MIL-STD-810 (currently Rev H with Change Notice 1), MIL-DTL-901 (currently Rev E), MIL-STD-167 (currently Rev 1A with Validation Notice 1), and MIL-HDBK-2164 (currently Rev A),

IOU must remain fully operational through momentary power interruptions from the selected power source. If all AC power is lost, the IOU will automatically restart within 30 seconds following restoration of at least one power source. Adequate cooling must be maintained in any power-on condition.

User Interfaces, Routing, Processing:

IOU must adhere to a defined set of core networking standards. The unit must ensure full compliance with the foundational protocols for internetworking, including IPv4 (RFC 791) and IPv6 (RFC 8200). To support efficient one-to-many data distribution, the IOU must implement IP Multicasting (RFC 1112). For high-availability and fault tolerance, the IOU must also support the Parallel Redundancy Protocol (PRP) in accordance with IEC 62439-3.

Fiber optic cables connecting the IOU to shipboard networks will be supplied by the shipbuilders and will utilize a four-fiber cable per MIL-PRF-85045/18 with a fiber cable class of single mode per MIL-PRF-49291/7.

Reliance on legacy hardware and proprietary data currently limits the Navy's ability to use open competition. Updating the design to include commercially available components will eliminate these constraints and significantly reduce lifecycle costs.

Phase I:
Develop a concept for an IOU that meets the requirements described above. Demonstrate through modeling and simulation and other supporting documentation the efficacy of the proposed system design for satisfying prototype system requirements. If the Phase I Option is exercised, include the initial design specifications and capabilities or description to build a prototype solution in Phase II.

Phase II:
Construct, test, and deliver a prototype in accordance with the above Description that can be inserted in a network lab environment to verify continuity and throughput of all required signal types with legacy connections. Ensure that the prototype must demonstrate adequate cooling capability under sustained heavy loading and meet or exceed IP54 as verified by testing in accordance with IEC 60529 (Ingress Protection codes for electrical equipment enclosures) and MIL-STD-1399 (Shipboard Electric Plants), paragraph 300F.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
With enclosures that maintain adequate cooling while maintaining IP54 protection, IOUs may continue to be used in a wide variety of shipboard spaces and use could be more readily expanded to commercial industrial operations. Future designs could investigate expanding processing and storage capability at IOUs to create distributed processing capabilities across industrial networks or translate hardware signals to a cloud architecture. Additionally, IOUs could be tailored and optimized for specific activities or modified for use in other types of networks or at higher classification levels.

Support the Navy in transitioning the IOU technology for fleet-wide use, providing the necessary equipment, training, and logistical documentation.

Potential commercial applications for an IOU include commercial maritime systems, offshore extraction, and advanced industrial processes.

• European Parliament & Council of the European Union. “Directive 2011/65/EU on the restriction of the use of certain hazardous substances in electrical and electronic equipment.” EUR-Lex., June 8, 2011, Official Journal of the European Union. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=celex:32011L0065
• McHale, J. “Demanding high-speed I/O.” Military & Aerospace Electronics, Volume 20, September 2009, pp. 34-37, 42. https://www.militaryaerospace.com/computers/article/16713292/demanding-highspeed-io
• Keller, J. “Gigabit Ethernet Data Multiplex System installed on Navy destroyer for shipboard networking.” Military & Aerospace Electronics, Volume 23, February 2012., p. 27. https://www.militaryaerospace.com/home/article/16714441/gigabit-ethernet-data-multiplex-system-installed-on-navy-destroyer-for-shipboard-networking

title: TRIAGE-X: Autonomous Casualty Triage and Treatment in Chemically Contaminated Mass Casualty Events
summary: Develop and demonstrate capability with autonomous medical triage systems to recognize chemical toxidromes and physically deliver the corresponding antidote or life-saving intervention.
description:
Objective:
Develop and demonstrate capability with autonomous medical triage systems to recognize chemical toxidromes and physically deliver the corresponding antidote or life-saving intervention.

Description:
DARPA seeks innovative approaches to autonomous chemical, biological, radioactive, and nuclear (CBRN) triage that measurably improve casualty survival and increase the effective capacity of a medical response during CBRN disasters. Early situational awareness and timely treatment is a matter of life and death in battlefield and disaster medical triage. Responder vulnerability in hazardous environments caused by CBRN attacks adds significant difficulty to the medical response. When a mass casualty incident (MCI) occurs within a chemically contaminated area, the medical response is hindered by uncertainty while the threat is assessed and characterized. To ensure safety of the responders, they must don protective equipment before entry, delaying initial assessment, triage, and treatment with life-saving interventions (LSIs). Personal protective equipment (PPE) also imposes a physiological and functional penalty on responders resulting in slower movement, higher energy expenditure, heat stress, impaired respiration, and reduced manual dexterity; these penalties further impede responders’ ability to perform life-saving interventions. Effective stabilization occurs in the cold zone after casualties have been decontaminated [1,2], compounding the delay to evacuation and definitive care. The DARPA Triage Challenge (DTC) has demonstrated that autonomous air and ground systems, using standoff sensors, can locate casualties, characterize injury patterns, and support triage prioritization in realistic MCI conditions [3]. Using DTC triage support capabilities as a starting point, this solicitation aims to extend capabilities to operating in chemically hazardous environments where injury patterns have distinct signatures or toxidromes. Success here extends proven autonomous triage into the one of the most challenging settings where human entry is dangerous and delayed, and where early antidote delivery most directly determines casualty survival [4].Proposed systems should be able to locate and assess casualties for traumatic injuries and chemical toxidromes, generate triage recommendations, and deliver appropriate initial treatments to reverse, stabilize, or prevent the toxic effects of chemicals. Solutions should be designed for realistic operational use in difficult terrain under challenging environmental conditions. DARPA does not prescribe a specific platform, sensor suite, or level of autonomy. Offerors are encouraged to propose the human-machine teaming arrangement that best improves decision quality and casualty outcomes, and to define how their system fails safely when conditions exceed its competence. Approaches should be realistic in scope, repurposed within the period of performance, and grounded in how CBRN mass casualty response actually unfolds.At minimum, the effort shall deliver a demonstrated prototype that detects at least two representative chemical toxidromes and applies appropriate initial treatments for the assessed toxidrome following human-in-the-loop treatment approval.

Phase I:
Phase I work is expected to have been completed before award. Proposers must submit evidence that their existing prototype can:• Autonomously find and localize casualties and report their location to within 2m• Assess trauma patterns and assign a trauma triage category• Perform accurate standoff vital-signs assessment, including at minimum heart rate and respiratory rate • Operate at scale o At least 20 casualties in a single scenario o Perform assessment in <90 seconds for each casualtyo Survey a 30,000sqft area without battery change• Operate across diverse, realistic environments: indoor and outdoor, daytime and nighttime, ideally (but not required) in adverse weather conditions (rain, smoke)• Produce a human-interpretable output through a graphical interface that conveys casualty locations and priorities of care.• System must be portable. All components should be easily transported by a vehicle or drone.Capability demonstration:A written technical description or published report supported by data and video(s) demonstrating the prototype performing the capabilities above in the stated environments are required (provided via link).

Phase II:
Building on the feasibility demonstrated in the documentation above, the Phase II effort will extend their qualified baseline system to assess and treat chemical toxidromes. In this effort, performers will develop, integrate, and validate a prototype autonomous chemical casualty triage system and demonstrate it in a relevant environment. The system shall identify casualties, assess them for life threatening and other traumatic injuries, assess casualties for chemical toxidromes, and provide relevant physical treatments. Requirements: Performers shall develop the capability to assess and treat at least two chemical agent categories from Table 1. Agent detection is out of scope for this effort. Treatment recommendations and options for each casualty shall be presented through a graphical interface to responders. Treatment decisions will always be made by humans.

Intervention Delivery

• * The platform must physically administer treatment appropriate to the chosen toxidrome according to table 1 on a manikin.
• * Final demonstration requires the system payload and automation to administer treatment to at least 5 casualties in succession without battery changes or re-supply.

Platform, Environment, and Autonomy

• * Platform-agnostic: Autonomous UAV and UGVs. Performer may choose the sensor suite (excluding chemical-specific sensors). System must demonstrate safe physical interaction with casualties represented by high-fidelity manikins.
• † A single robust platform must operate across and transition between realistic environments — difficult terrain, inside and outside of buildings, and potentially subterranean settings. Dedicated single-environment platforms are not sought.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:

summary: Mature commercial and dual-use technologies that detect, track, identify, or defeat small low-flying drones (Group 1 and Group 2 unmanned aerial systems) in hostile or contested areas.
description:
Objective:
Mature commercial and dual-use technologies that detect, track, identify, or defeat small low-flying drones (Group 1 and Group 2 unmanned aerial systems) in hostile or contested areas.

Description:
Inexpensive, highly maneuverable, commercially available unmanned aerial systems (UAS) threaten tactical forces, critical infrastructure, and installations. Current defenses are limited by cost, by the operator attention they require, and by their vulnerability to countermeasures. A capability gap against Group 1 and Group 2 UAS remains.

This topic seeks mature or maturing technology at any point in the counter-UAS kill chain. The three areas below are where capability is most needed. They are examples. A proposal may address one area, more than one, or a gap not listed here.

Detection and Tracking. Detect and hold track on highly agile targets in cluttered low-altitude airspace. The proposer selects the sensing modality. Approaches that hold track when the target is not emitting are preferred. Solutions that require permanent site infrastructure or mains power, including fixed perimeter sensor installations, are out of scope for this area. The system must move with the force.

Identification and Decision Support. Classify and identify unauthorized platforms and support an engagement decision. Processing must run on tactical computing hardware carried or emplaced with the force. Proposals should describe a pathway to interoperate with existing command and control. Conformance to a named standard is not required at this stage and will not be scored.

Mitigation and Defeat. Kinetic, non-kinetic, or cyber approaches that defeat hostile UAS in remote tactical theaters and in densely populated areas. Proposals must address collateral effects.

Operating preferences. The operating environment is denied, contested, and unattended. The four conditions below are preferences, not eligibility requirements.

Every proposal must state where it stands against each one.

(a) The system does not require the target to emit radio frequency (RF) energy. Passive RF may be part of a solution; the preference is that track holds when the target is silent.

(b) The system does not radiate. The Government favors kinetic and cyber defeat over approaches that require the friendly system to emit. Jamming, active illumination, and transmission into a target's control or navigation link are in scope. A proposal that uses any of them must say so and describe the operational effect.

(c) The system does not require cloud services or reachback. Training and analytics may occur off-platform. The processing that produces the operational output should run on the platform, and the system should continue to function with all external network interfaces disabled.

(d) The system does not require a dedicated operator, meaning no person whose only task is attending it. Human judgment over the use of force is expected and is not addressed by this preference.

Out of scope: work requiring classified access or a facility clearance at the time of award, and approaches that depend on cooperative identification, including Remote ID broadcast.

Phase I:
This topic solicits Direct-to-Phase-II (DP2) proposals only. Direct to Phase II proposers shall submit documentation showing that Phase I-equivalent feasibility has already been achieved outside the SBIR/STTR program. Adequate documentation is a written record of at least one test of the proposed approach stating the conditions under which the test was conducted, the dates, the target, threat, or surrogate used, the measured result, and how it was measured.Test data, technical reports, and third-party evaluation metrics are acceptable. A system design alone is not sufficient. A self-declared technology readiness level unsupported by a documented test is not sufficient.

As required by the DoW solicitation, the feasibility documented may not rest solely upon, or logically extend from, prior or ongoing federally funded SBIR or STTR work; the proposing firm and/or the principal investigator must have substantially performed the work relied upon; and the firm must demonstrate ownership or licensure of the associated intellectual property prior to proposal submission.

Phase II:
Phase II is a major research and development effort. Performers refine the Phase I concept into an operational prototype that demonstrates real-world functionality. The primary deliverable is a functional system, software package, or physical prototype ready for test and evaluation in a militarily relevant or simulated field environment. The technology shall reach TRL 6 by the end of Phase II.

The period of performance is twelve months rather than the twenty-four the announcement allows. The intent is to move a demonstrated capability to a transition decision within one year. Proposals should be scoped to that schedule.

The Government may host a showcase about six months after award. Attendance is by invitation and is based on end user interest in the capability. It is not required of every performer. Performers shall provide operational evidence supporting a follow-on funding decision whether or not they are invited.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
Commercial applications are those in which the equipment deploys with a team rather than being installed at a site: temporary airspace security for outdoor events, venues, and construction or energy sites; convoy, executive, and site-survey protection; wildfire, disaster, and critical infrastructure response; and mobile detection kits for law enforcement and allied partners. Detection, tracking, and identification technologies have a direct commercial market in these roles. Authority to mitigate or defeat unmanned aircraft in the United States is limited by statute to covered federal entities. A defeat-focused proposal is not expected to show a near-term domestic commercial market for that function.

Military applications include integration into point-defense systems for tactical units, forward operating bases, and naval vessel protection platforms, which may be funded via non-SBIR/STTR acquisition budgets.

References:
• Congressional Research Service. Department of Defense Counter Unmanned Aircraft Systems: Background and Issues for Congress. Report R48477. https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R48477
• Statement of General Michael E. Kurilla, Commander, U.S. Central Command, before the Senate Armed Services Committee on the posture of U.S. Central Command, 10 June 2025.
• U.S. Department of Defense Counter-Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Strategy (2021). https://media.defense.gov/2021/Jan/07/2002561080/-1/-1/1/DEPARTMENT-OF-DEFENSE-COUNTER-SMALL-UNMANNED-AIRCRAFT-SYSTEMS-STRATEGY.PDF
